This gives more scalable, yet accurate, algorithms for online inference about the latent state and prediction of future observations. Finally, we derive a novel expectation maximization procedure to learn from the data the covariance matrix underlying the latent-utility representation of the multinomial probit. We investigate the performance of the proposed methods on simulated data and on a real dataset of reservations from an online booking platform.

nominations.title: Randomization-Based Nonparanormal Adjusted Marginal Inference
nominations.authors: Leticia W\"uthrich, Mark Baillie, Susanne Dandl
nominations.abstract: Adjusting for prognostic baseline covariates in the analysis of randomized controlled trials is recommended to increase the precision of treatment effect estimates. Such adjustment, however, introduces a complication known as noncollapsibility: for effect measures such as the log-odds or log-hazard ratio, the estimated treatment effect becomes conditional instead of marginal. Methods that target a marginal estimand even after covariate adjustment have been developed, but typically rely on population-based inference, which assumes patients are randomly sampled from some larger population, rarely true in practice. Such methods have been shown to inflate type I error, particularly in small samples or when many covariates are adjusted for. Inference based on randomization requires no such assumption, as it relies on the randomization scheme, which is known exactly, yielding a test that is exact even in finite samples. We present a randomization-based test for covariate-adjusted marginal treatment effects, built on nonparanormal adjusted marginal inference, applicable to continuous, binary, ordinal, and time-to-event outcomes. In simulation studies, this test controls type I error where the standard Wald test does not. Applied to 20 historical phase III time-to-event randomized trials, the covariate-adjusted estimator achieves precision gains comparable to an existing competitor method.

nominations.title: FAST: Functional Adaptive Sensing and Testing for Quickest Change Detection
nominations.authors: Peiyao Liu, Jie Guo, Zhijun Wang, Xueru Zhang, Nan Chen
nominations.abstract: Quickest change detection (QCD) is studied for partially observed functional data streams. At each sampling epoch, a function is realized over a continuous domain, but its values can be observed at only a fixed number of locations. At an unknown change point, the functional mean undergoes a shift that is assumed to admit a sparse representation in a localized basis. We propose Functional Adaptive Sensing and Testing (FAST), which jointly estimates the unknown post-change parameter, selects sensing locations, and performs sequential detection. A minimax lower bound on the worst-case detection delay is derived under an average-run-length constraint. A non-asymptotic estimation-error bound is established for the policy-dependent observations induced by adaptive sensing. Under the stated regularity conditions, FAST is first-order asymptotically optimal when sensing subsets are optimized exactly. Simulations and a wildfire case study demonstrate the performance of the proposed procedure.

nominations.title: TRAIL-IRL: Crossed Reward-Temperature Mixtures for Unlabeled Trajectory Clustering
nominations.authors: Yichen Zhu, Guanhua Fang, Ming Zheng
nominations.abstract: Different paths need not imply different preferences, trajectories also differ in how randomly actions are chosen. Many multi-reward inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) methods assume common action randomness and can confound it with preference heterogeneity. We introduce TRAIL-IRL, which clusters unlabeled trajectories using rewards for preferences and temperatures for action randomness. Its crossed mixture pairs each reward with a shared set of temperature levels, allowing action regularity to vary within preference groups. With centered and normalized rewards in a known finite-state environment, we establish the identifiability conditions under which the distribution of sufficiently long trajectories determines rewards, temperatures, mixing weights, and class counts up to relabeling. Under the same conditions and reward constraints, common-temperature reward mixtures with the same component count cannot reproduce a crossed mixture with multiple temperatures. We develop a generalized expectation-maximization algorithm and select class counts using the Bayesian information criterion (BIC). Simulations show improved predictive fit, reward recovery, and trajectory classification over common-temperature mixtures with the same component count. For 140 bird-year trajectories from 79 white storks, BIC favors four reward classes and three temperature levels over common-temperature candidates. Younger birds have higher posterior membership probabilities for a southwestward migration class, whereas older birds have higher probabilities for a northern retention class. Within reward classes, higher temperatures are associated with more variable movement directions and positions farther ahead along the migration route, consistent with social information use and collective sensing.

nominations.title: Greedy Empirical Bayes for Density Estimation
nominations.authors: Taole Sha, Shibo Yu, Edwin Fong
nominations.abstract: Bayesian nonparametric density estimation is challenging in high dimensions, where traditional approaches like the Dirichlet process (DP) mixture rely on computationally intensive Markov chain Monte Carlo or approximations. We introduce the partition posterior bootstrap (PPB), where a flexible prior is constructed by smoothing a DP over a partition of the sample space. Conditioned on this partition, exact posterior sampling reduces to a simple Bayesian bootstrap-like algorithm. Importantly, we select the partition using a greedy empirical Bayes (GEB) algorithm which scales to high dimensions and large sample sizes. GEB greedily maximizes the closed-form marginal likelihood via local split decisions arising naturally from its factorization, yielding an adaptive binary tree partition. Our key theoretical result is that the GEB tree belongs to an admissible family with high probability, splitting all identifiable signals while avoiding over-splitting noise. As a result, the PPB posterior with the GEB tree attains adaptive contraction rates. Our theory holds under weak, verifiable assumptions, which we demonstrate in numerous examples. Empirically, PPB delivers accurate density estimates and uncertainty quantification at a fraction of the computational cost of other approaches, making it a practical off-the-shelf choice for high-dimensional Bayesian density estimation with theoretical guarantees.

nominations.title: Sequential Conditional Paired-Sample Testing with Applications to Online Monitoring
nominations.authors: Xiaoyi Zheng, Hong Zhang
nominations.abstract: We study sequential conditional paired-sample testing, where observations arrive over time and the goal is to continuously assess whether two conditional distributions are equal given a common set of covariates. This problem arises naturally in model monitoring, where distributional changes must be detected without a prespecified terminal sample size, and in online comparisons, where responses are compared conditional on subject-level characteristics. We propose SCPT, an anytime-valid testing procedure for conditional distributions based on sequentially constructed conditional kernel discrepancy statistics and test martingales. The proposed method is nonparametric and accommodates a broad class of data-generating processes beyond the i.i.d. setting. We establish time-uniform Type I error control and derive asymptotic power guarantees under suitable regularity conditions. We also develop several useful extensions to address different needs, including testing under broader dependence structures, comparisons involving multiple auxiliary streams, and conditional goodness-of-fit testing. Simulations and real-data experiments show that SCPT effectively detects conditional distributional differences in streaming data, demonstrating its practical utility in a wide range of real-world applications.

nominations.title: Inference for Heterogeneous Treatment Effects with Deep Survival Learners
nominations.authors: Sattwik Ghosal, Xuran Meng, Yuming Sun, Yi Li
nominations.abstract: Conditional average treatment effects (CATEs) provide a principled framework for assessing treatment-effect heterogeneity and identifying patients who may benefit from an intervention. For survival outcomes, CATEs may also evolve over time and pose challenges for estimation and inference. Existing methods can accommodate complex covariate heterogeneity but often fail to exploit shared temporal structure or provide valid inference for time-varying treatment effects and their contrasts. We propose a deep survival learning framework that combines neural networks for nonparametric covariate effects with a shared spline representation of temporal variation, enabling joint estimation of CATE trajectories. Using doubly robust pseudo-outcomes and sample splitting, we establish nonasymptotic oracle bounds accounting for network and temporal approximation, nuisance estimation, and optimization errors. Our theory shows that exploiting shared temporal structure yields sharper error bounds for temporal contrasts than those derived from separate time-specific estimators. For inference, we develop a subsampled ensemble procedure and establish asymptotic normality for pointwise CATEs, temporal contrasts, and covariate contrasts, including temporal contrasts over shrinking time intervals. Under suitable regularity and bias-control conditions, consistent infinitesimal jackknife variance estimators yield asymptotically valid confidence intervals. Simulations evaluate estimation accuracy, interval coverage, and sensitivity to temporal dimension and basis mismatch. An application to lung cancer survival data illustrates the framework's ability to characterize heterogeneous treatment benefits over time.

nominations.title: Inference after coding agents
nominations.authors: Florian Gunsilius, David Van Dijcke, Kaspar W\"uthrich
nominations.abstract: Empirical research is changing rapidly as AI coding agents are becoming increasingly proficient in every step of it, from writing code to manipulating data. We argue that while the potential of coding agents for science is vast, their use in hypothesis testing poses a substantial threat to classical inference, as these agents enable a supercharged form of selective inference. In particular, we argue that coding agents carrying out empirical research introduce a new type of post-selection inference that combines human-like, open-ended search over an implicit space of estimators with programmatic replayability of both the selection and the estimation process. Indeed, we find that on simulated data with zero effects, four frontier agents report significant p-values between 54% and 98% of the time when asked to produce a compelling finding. We propose a simple procedure for detecting and correcting these distortions. After an agent has completed its analysis, we reset and replay it on subsamples of the data to estimate the agent's relative probability of selecting that analysis when it looks statistically favorable. For agents with stable selection behavior, the resulting corrected test is asymptotically valid and consistent conditional on selection. Importantly, the correction is learned from the black-box agent's actual choices rather than a model of how it searches, so it remains valid even as AI technology continues to evolve rapidly. In simulations, the correction robustly lowers the high false rejection rates to near the nominal 5%. We illustrate the method on applications from two published papers.

nominations.title: Fold Weighting for Cross-Validation Under Continuous Distributional Drift
nominations.authors: Yegor Baranovski
nominations.abstract: Cross-validation weights all folds equally, so under drift the oldest folds count as much as the newest. We model drift by a H\"older condition in total variation distance and give finite-sample bounds on the excess deployment risk of the configuration that sliding-window cross-validation selects. Each bound splits into drift, estimation, and validation-noise terms. With equal weights the drift terms saturate as the record grows. With fold weights fixed in advance, the drift terms become weighted averages, which shrink as weight moves toward deployment. The noise term grows as the weights concentrate and shrinks with the batch size. The drift terms are linear in the weights and the noise term is convex, so minimizing the bound over the weights is a convex problem. Applications to U.S. earnings and flight delays show both sides of this trade-off. Weight on recent folds pays off when a change in the best predictor persists and each period has many observations, and equal weights do best when changes are short-lived.

nominations.title: When Is Membership Graded? Identifiability and Resolution Limits of a Graded Gaussian Mixture Model
nominations.authors: Sie Hendrata Dharmawan, Peter Chin
nominations.abstract: Mixed-membership models describe each unit as a graded blend of latent types. Before the blend is interpreted, the data should be able to rule out the simpler story in which every unit belongs to a single type. We ask when they can, in a scalar graded Gaussian mixture model, in which each observation is a Beta-weighted convex combination of independent Gaussian draws from two types, the mechanism behind functional mixed-membership models and the normal compositional model. The model is identifiable, unequal variances included, but the identifying information sits in the far tails of the marginal. For the symmetric model we give a closed-form hard-membership mixture that matches the graded marginal in five cumulants, and a Le Cam bound turns it into a certified sample size below which no test separates graded from hard membership with summed error under one half. The threshold is governed by the concentration $c$ relative to $c_0\approx d^2$, where $d$ is the type half-separation in within-type standard deviations. At $d=3$ it is about 2,600 observations at $c=3$ and 77,000 at $c=6$. Most of the difficulty comes from learning $c$. On 100 simulated datasets with graded membership, a correctly specified posterior under the default priors of a published Bayesian sampler for this model class reports hard membership every time, a weak prior gives intervals for the concentration spanning orders of magnitude, and the sampler's own answers depend on where it starts.

nominations.title: Simultaneous analysis of approximate leave-one-out cross-validation and mean-field inference II: General convex penalties
nominations.authors: Pierre C Bellec
nominations.abstract: For smooth penalties and group Lasso, analyzed approximate leave-one-out (ALO) cross-validation by comparing its weights with the trace correction used in mean-field inference. For a $C^2$ penalty $R$, the matrix entering these corrections is $A=[\nabla^2R(\widehat b)+X^TDX]^{-1}$, where $\widehat b$ is the full-data estimator and $D$ is the diagonal matrix of fitted loss curvatures; for group Lasso, the penalty and loss curvatures are first restricted to the active support before taking the pseudoinverse. The obstacle to extending this argument to general convex penalties was the lack of an explicit formula for the matrix $A$ entering these corrections. For every finite-valued strongly convex penalty, we construct such a matrix from ordinary derivatives of the penalty response at the observed subgradient. Its projection--pseudoinverse formula separates the response space and penalty curvature, fixed by conditioning, from the explicit design dependence. This supplies the missing ingredient to extend the probabilistic argument of Part~I. The construction recovers the inverse Hessian for smooth penalties and the active-group inverse for group Lasso, including inactive boundary groups. In the proportional regime, for Gaussian designs with general positive-definite covariance and covariance-scaled strong convexity, we obtain unconditional bounds comparing both ALO and mean-field predictions with exact leave-one-out predictions in regression and single-index models. The expected average squared prediction error is $O(n^{-1})$, and the expected absolute criterion error is $O(n^{-1/2})$, under bounded, 1-Lipschitz loss scores and suitable test functions. The matrix and ALO weights use only observed data; the mean-field correction additionally uses the design covariance. The construction, recovery identities and statistical guarantees are formalized in Lean~4.

nominations.title: Training Neural Networks to be Locally Adaptive
nominations.authors: Bilol Banerjee, Soham Sarkar
nominations.abstract: Deep neural networks fitted by global empirical risk minimization commit to a single model for the entire covariate space. In a regression problem, if the regression function $f_0$ is inhomogeneous --- varying rapidly in one region, while being nearly flat in another --- no single model can be appropriate everywhere, and the fit degrades where the function varies most rapidly. Here we study an alternative in which, instead of fitting the network globally, we fit it locally. For each query point $x$, a \emph{local neural network} is trained on the $k$ nearest-neighbours of $x$ alone, making the training sample and the fitted function query-dependent. We analyze the performance of the resulting estimator through a localization approach, establishing that the pointwise risk of the estimator with an appropriate choice of $k$ attains the rate $n^{-2\alpha/(2\alpha+d^{*})}$, up to logarithmic factors, when $f_0$ is locally $\alpha$-H\"older with $\alpha\in(0,1]$ and the covariates are supported on a $d^{*}$-dimensional manifold embedded in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$. A matching Le Cam lower bound shows that this rate is pointwise minimax optimal. However, the local rate-optimality requires $k$ to be calibrated to the smoothness of $f_0$, which is unknown in practice. We therefore provide a locally adaptive choice of $k$ that makes the neural network adapt to the local H\"older exponent of $f_0$ and to the intrinsic dimension simultaneously, both of which are potentially varying over the covariate domain. An extensive simulation study demonstrates the dominance of the locally adaptive neural network over a globally trained network and several state-of-the-art methods.

nominations.title: Anytime-valid inference for conditional hazard and survival functions with streaming data
nominations.authors: Eni Musta, Valentin Patilea
nominations.abstract: We consider the nonparametric estimation of the conditional hazard, cumulative hazard and survival functions of a time-to-event variable from streaming data subject to censoring, truncation, or a cure fraction. A time-to-event model is a map from the distribution of the latent variables to that of the observed ones. For a large class of models this map has an explicit inverse, and the conditional hazard is the ratio of the density of the exactly observed durations to an at-risk function. Both are estimated by one-pass learners, in which each observation contributes once and is never revised, such as recursive kernel, series and histogram estimators. Our main result is an asymptotic confidence band sequence for the conditional hazard at a fixed covariate value, uniform in time and in the sample size, which allows monitoring after a burn-in, and stopping at a data-dependent time. The band can shrink at the optimal uniform rate up to a logarithmic factor. Bands for the cumulative hazard and the survival function follow. In simulations, a fixed-sample band inspected repeatedly fails in about half of the streams, while the miscoverage of the recommended bands stays below, or close to, the nominal level.

nominations.title: Bivariate Renyi Tsallis Divergence
nominations.authors: Suramya Surendran, Rajesh G
nominations.abstract: In this paper, a bivariate extension of the differential Renyi Tsallis divergence is introduced for comparing two absolutely continuous bivariate probability distributions. Fundamental properties of the proposed divergence are studied, including non negativity, pseudo additivity under component wise independence, and invariance under monotone and nonsingular linear transformations. Relationships with Renyi, Tsallis, alpha, Bhattacharyya, and Hellinger divergence measures are also established. A sensitivity analysis is performed to compare the Renyi, Tsallis and Renyi Tsallis divergences under the Marshall Olkin and Gumbel type bivariate exponential models, taking the magnitude of Kendall's rank correlation coefficient as a common scale for dependence. The proposed measure is further developed for bivariate order statistics, with particular emphasis on the joint distribution of the minimum and maximum order statistics for several lifetime distributions, including exponential, Weibull, Pareto, and Rayleigh models. When the underlying distributions are unknown, a nonparametric estimator is constructed using bivariate Gaussian kernel density estimators with plug in bandwidth selection. The proposed estimator is applied to a real life dataset and bootstrap resampling is used to assess estimation uncertainty. The results show the applicability of the proposed divergence for comparing bivariate distributions and indicate that its finite sample performance depends on the order parameter and the distributions being compared.

nominations.title: Exact and Approximate Maximum Likelihood Estimation for Multivariate Diffusions under High-Frequency Sampling
nominations.authors: Duy Nguyen
nominations.abstract: We establish the asymptotic theory of the exact maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) for discretely observed multivariate ergodic diffusions under high-frequency, long-span sampling, solving an open problem posed by \citet{YCW2019} and \citet{Li2013}. The drift may grow linearly, and the volatility is bounded away from zero and either bounded or proportional to $1+|x|$. When the sampling interval decays polynomially, the exact MLE is consistent, asymptotically normal and efficient, with rates $\sqrt{n\Delta_n}$ for drift and $\sqrt n$ for diffusion parameters. Under an additional condition on ergodic averages, and when the time span $n\Delta_n$ also grows polynomially, its moments converge as well. The proof never analyzes the exact likelihood directly: it shows that a closed-form density expansion of sufficiently high order is uniformly accurate in relative terms at every observed transition, so that the two log-likelihoods differ by $o_P(1)$ uniformly in the parameter. The same argument yields accuracy conditions under which an approximate likelihood is asymptotically equivalent to the exact one; in particular, the approximate MLE of Yang, Chen and Wan converges to the true parameter. For the delta-expansion estimator of fixed order $K\ge1$, we derive the leading bias explicitly. It shows that $n\Delta_n^{K+1}\to0$ cannot be weakened when the bias constant is nonzero, and that the bias falls on the drift parameters for even $K$ and on the diffusion parameters for odd $K$. Monte Carlo experiments confirm the predicted biases.

nominations.title: Covariate-Indexed Inclusion Probabilities on Unbalanced Panels
nominations.authors: Paul Schneider
nominations.abstract: We estimate the probability that an item with given covariates belongs to a set when the cross-section changes over time and items and periods are dependent. We propose two convex models whose fitted probabilities are nonnegative by construction and remain valid whatever the dependence between items, for which we establish consistency, finite-sample bounds and limit distributions for serially dependent panels. One suits events of moderate or high probability, the other rare events, and half the disagreement between their fits estimates a lower bound on the misspecification error of the worse fit, without knowledge of the true probabilities. On monthly US stock failures, the rare-event model predicts better than the ordinary logit and the classical failure logit. With the eight classical predictors, most of the gain comes from basis functions of the rank angle of each predictor and summary.

nominations.title: Testing the Pareto law through a Stein-Laplace characterization
nominations.authors: Deepesh Bhati, Bruno Ebner, Sakshi Khandelwal
nominations.abstract: A Stein--Laplace characterization yields two closed-form goodness-of-fit statistics for the Pareto type-I family with unknown shape and known lower endpoint. The signed integral statistic $T_n$ has a standard normal limit after studentization, but explicit non-Pareto alternatives show that it is not omnibus consistent. The integrated squared discrepancy $S_n$ yields a consistent test against every fixed non-Pareto alternative on the specified support with a finite, positive logarithmic moment. We derive the weighted chi-square null limit of $nS_n$ and give conditions for an asymptotically valid parametric-bootstrap and plug-in covariance-operator method. The latter uses Nystr\"om eigenvalue approximation to avoid repeated sample generation and parameter estimation. A large Monte Carlo comparison study shows competitive performance relative to existing procedures in the literature. In the paired study, the two calibrations have similar empirical power, with slightly higher small-sample rejection rates for the bootstrap in some settings. In the timing experiment, covariance-operator calibration is approximately $28$--$37$ times faster at $n=200$. An exploratory threshold-sensitivity analysis of Danish fire-insurance losses illustrates the dependence of Pareto goodness-of-fit conclusions on the specified tail region.

nominations.title: Identifiability of latent variable models with flexible latent distributions
nominations.authors: Chengyu Cui, Gongjun Xu
nominations.abstract: Latent variable models are popularly used to characterize dependence among many observed variables through underlying latent variables. Recent advances in statistics and machine learning methods have encouraged growing interest in studying latent variable models with flexible latent distributions that capture complex latent structures. This flexibility, however, raises a fundamental question of whether model parameters can be identified when the latent distribution is unknown and must itself be learned. In this paper, we show that exact identifiability fails almost everywhere, in the sense that distinct but arbitrarily close pairs of model parameters and latent distributions can yield exactly the same distribution for the observed variables. Nonetheless, the resulting identification ambiguity is small. In particular, we prove that the identification ambiguity, measured by the diameter of the set of parameters inducing the same marginal distribution, vanishes at a superpolynomial rate of $\exp\{-c(\log p)^2\}$ as the number of observed variables $p$ grows. Building on this result, we show that the failure of exact identifiability need not preclude consistent estimation or valid inference of the model parameters and latent distribution. These results suggest that, when many variables are observed, the identifiability issue is far less of an obstacle to estimation and inference in latent variable models than is commonly expected.

nominations.title: Asymptotics of Gibbs Posterior Measures on Infinite-Dimensional Hypothesis Spaces
nominations.authors: Terje Mildner
nominations.abstract: We prove almost sure contraction rates and consistency for Gibbs posterior measures on arbitrary hypothesis spaces, in general infinite dimensional, under dependent data, nonadditive and time-dependent losses and learning rates, misspecified models, and unattainable minimisers of the limiting objective. In particular, we develop a novel proof approach in contraction rate theory by studying the asymptotics of Gibbs measures through Lorentz spaces, real interpolation theory, and Laplace transforms dispensing with testing or variational formulations which are unavailable in the considered generality. As a consequence we obtain almost sure contraction rates for dominated Bayes and fractional Bayes posterior measures in the same generality, extending existing theory on misspecified Bayesian inference. Furthermore, we demonstrate our theoretical results on novel applications to Gibbs posteriors for Dirichlet process priors with a nonadditive Wasserstein metric loss function under ergodic, non-Markovian observables.

nominations.title: The Online LSTM Prediction Models and The Term Structure of Predictions
nominations.authors: Christian Gourieroux, Joann Jasiak, Cheng Zhong
nominations.abstract: We examine and illustrate the properties of the Long Short Term Memory (LSTM) prediction models applied online to stationary inputs. We discuss the effects of: a) the network architecture that defines the admissible prediction functions, b) the objective function used to measure the prediction accuracy, and c) the Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) algorithm. We also study the prediction optimality, the term structure of predictions, the filtered memory dynamics. We also introduce a set of diagnostic tools for memory-based prediction models that focus on the estimated dynamics of the hidden states.

nominations.title: Estimation and Model Selection in Factor Models with Long Memory
nominations.authors: Dominik Ammon, Tobias Hartl, Rolf Tschernig
nominations.abstract: Panels in economics, finance and climate science are often driven by common components that differ in memory, such as common trends, cycles, or joint shocks. We study approximate factor models whose common factors are fractionally integrated with heterogeneous and unknown memory and develop the asymptotic theory of principal components for the panel in levels. Our theory builds on the eigenvalues of the sample covariance matrix being ordered by memory asymptotically: a nonstationary factor group with memory $d>1/2$ generates eigenvalues of order $NT^{2d-1}$, whereas stationary factors generate eigenvalues of order $N$. Principal components estimate the factors consistently up to rotation, while adjacent factor groups are separated at a rate given by their memory gap. The information criteria of Bai and Ng remain consistent for the total number of factors, with their penalties acting as thresholds on eigenvalues that are asymptotically ordered by factor memory. When the nonstationary factors lose their variance advantage, estimation in levels remains consistent, whereas after differencing the factors can become undetectable. A Monte Carlo study shows that factor-number selection in levels tolerates more idiosyncratic noise than selection after first differencing. For monthly temperatures at $308$ European weather stations, our methods select two factors. The first is a persistent common warming factor. The estimated common component implies that 2021-2025 was $2.15^\circ\mathrm{C}$ warmer than 1960-1990, with the strongest warming in Eastern Europe. After first differencing, the criterion selects one factor, and loses regional heterogeneity as compared to the model in levels.

nominations.title: Nested logit: model structure and normalisation
nominations.authors: Stephane Hess
nominations.abstract: Nested logit remains a widely used model, especially in applied work. However, there remains substantial confusion surrounding the existence of different versions of the model, different normalisations for the same version, and different software implementations. This paper argues that the labels in common use, RU1 and RU2, and the name non-normalised nested logit (NNNL) itself, have contributed to the confusion. The model is written in two forms: one in which utilities are divided by the structural parameter of the nest that contains them, which is consistent with utility maximisation by construction, and one without that division, known as NNNL. The difference between these forms is not one of normalisation. Normalising at the top or at the bottom gives the same model, and NNNL is itself normalised. What distinguishes the forms is whether the division is performed. In short, normalisation changes the units, whereas division changes the model. The undivided form coincides with the utility-consistent one only under specific conditions, and otherwise is consistent with utility maximisation only under utilities other than those specified, in which generic coefficients become nest-specific. The paper highlights that RU1 has been used for three different specifications, compares how widely used software packages normalise and report their parameters, and illustrates the consequences with calculated examples. The recommendation is that models be described by what they do, rather than by these labels.

nominations.title: Long-Term Quantile Treatment Effects with Combined Experimental and Observational Data
nominations.authors: Nan Liu, Yanbo Liu, Yuya Sasaki, Yichong Zhang
nominations.abstract: This paper studies the identification, estimation, and inference of long-term quantile treatment effects (LTQTEs) when short-term experimental data are supplemented with long-term observational data. Under a latent unconfoundedness framework, we establish identification of the LTQTE curve and derive the corresponding efficient influence functions. Building on these influence functions, we propose a semiparametrically efficient estimation procedure and develop a multiplier bootstrap method for uniform inference on the LTQTE curve, yielding valid simultaneous confidence bands over a continuum of quantile indices.

nominations.title: Who sees the sea? Sea-view potential by fa\c{c}ade and floor from cadastral LoD1 models on the Costa del Sol
nominations.authors: Gabriel Rojo (CASAS.ES)
nominations.abstract: Views are among the most valued and least measured attributes of a home. We present an open-data method that estimates the sea-view potential of every free fa\c{c}ade of every residential building at three floors (ground, middle and top; other floors take the nearest of them), from cadastral footprints with floor counts and a national terrain model. Run for 158,060 buildings of 21 municipalities on Spain's Costa del Sol in under an hour on two cores, it finds that 52 % of buildings see some sea from their top floor and 36 % have an open view (20{\deg} or more). Traced over a LiDAR surface in a pilot, scores agree with the model's inside cadastral footprints (96.7 % of viewpoints in the same class at 20{\deg}), but structures the cadastre does not record lower the sea seen from the top floor by 6.1--9.0{\deg} on average. Against the photographs of 93 homes for sale, labelled blind by AI models of two developers with ties decided by the author, the score has an AUC of 0.80 (95 % CI 0.70--0.89; 0.81 against the first-round labels); at 20{\deg} it is sensitive (0.90) but not specific (0.45). Dwelling figures depend on how dwellings are allocated to fa\c{c}ades and floors: 42 % of dwellings are on a floor with open-view potential under the main rule, and 12--45 % across the allocation, geometry and vegetation scenarios tested. As an application, higher-income census sections tend to have more modelled view potential within municipalities, with uncertain size and fragile inference (about two effective clusters); on terrain alone the difference largely disappears. Code and fa\c{c}ade-level data reproduce the main results.

nominations.title: Clicks, Carbon, and Risk: Climate Attention, Persistent Financial Risk, and Real-Sector Activity
nominations.authors: Giovanni Angelini, Luca De Angelis
nominations.abstract: Do shifts in public climate concern alter persistent financial risk and subsequently matter for real activity? We combine daily U.S. sectoral equity returns with a monthly Climate Concern Index (CCI) constructed from internet search intensity and decomposed into adverse and transition-oriented components. GARCH-MIDAS estimates reveal substantial heterogeneity: adverse climate concern raises persistent volatility in carbon-intensive Energy activities, while transition-oriented attention tends to reduce persistent volatility in regulated Utilities, with important differences across sub-sectors. We then construct a persistent-risk differential between Energy and Utilities and examine its predictive content for sectoral real activity using local projections. Innovations associated with adverse climate concern precede declines in Oil and Gas industrial production and employment over the following quarters, while comparable Utilities responses are limited. The production result is preserved when the financial predictor is reconstructed using the more closely matched Oil, Gas, Coal equity sub-sector and remains economically similar across several robustness checks. Overall, the findings establish a link between climate concern, persistent sectoral financial risk, and subsequent real-sector activity.

nominations.title: Does the AI Reviewer Alleviate or Aggravate the Maintenance Burden? Evidence from GitHub Copilot Reviewer
nominations.authors: Feiyang (Amber), Xu, Poonacha K. Medappa, Murat M. Tunc
nominations.abstract: This study examines how AI-based code reviewers reshape contribution behavior and maintenance dynamics in open-source software (OSS) communities. AI reviewers provide scalable, fast, and standardized evaluations. They reshape contributions as well as maintainers' workload. Leveraging the introduction of GitHub Copilot Reviewer on GitHub as a natural experiment in 2025, we investigate how AI review affects maintainers' workload and review efficiency as well as contribution behavior. We find that repository maintainers initially face a sharp increase in PR submissions and a higher review workload after the adoption of the AI reviewer. Over time, human contributions decline while the increase in bot-generated PRs is sustained. Interestingly, survival analysis reveals that AI reviewers increase review efficiency for human PR contributions, whereas bot PRs take longer to review and merge. Our findings suggest that while AI reviewers increase review efficiency, they aggravate the maintenance burden by encouraging more code contributions via humans and bots.

nominations.title: OCCAM: Improved Single-Cell Representation Learning and Perturbation Effect Prediction
nominations.authors: Ihab Bendidi, Kian Kenyon-Dean, Alisandra K. Denton, Auguste Genovesio, Emmanuel Noutahi
nominations.abstract: Predicting the effects of genetic perturbations requires models that generalize beyond observed cell contexts and gene combinations. We introduce Occam, a multilayer perceptron (MLP) framework for representation learning and perturbation-effect prediction. Occam combines cell representations learned through denoising with gene interaction, text, and protein-sequence features. It achieves the highest aggregate representation scores for perturbation information and cell-type preservation with batch integration. In cross-context few-shot prediction, a perturbation and a cell context are each observed during training, but never together. Occam better captures the measured response patterns for these unobserved combinations than four retrained competitors or direct transfer of the same perturbation's measured effects from other training cell lines. Without fine-tuning, Occam best distinguishes perturbations among the evaluated models and simple baselines in cell lines held out from predictor training, across seen and unseen assays. Predicting expression levels accurately in these settings remains challenging. For double perturbations, which target two genes simultaneously, Occam composes learned single-gene responses to better capture the combined response and reduce expression error compared with competing models and summed single-gene effects. These gains extend to both strongly additive and weakly additive responses. Together, these results support simple MLPs for cell representation learning and perturbation-effect prediction across contexts and gene combinations.

nominations.title: Optimising Recruitment and Sample Allocation in Multi-Site Rare Disease Studies
nominations.authors: Farid Zare, Catherine Clancy, Tal Dattner, Martina Messina, Julian Teinert, Jack McGoldrick, Pavel Je\v{s}ina, Sabine Weller Gr{\o}nborg, Ute Spiekerkoetter, James J O'Byrne, Trine Tangeraas, Maria Luz Couce, Jos\'e A. Cocho, Javier de las Heras, Niklas Darin, Dorothea M\"oslinger, Peter Witters, Ina Knerr, Giancarlo La Marca, Ans T. van der Ploeg, Hidde H. Huidekoper, Terry G. J. Derks, Francjan J. van Spronsen, Sandra D. K Kingma, Anibh M. Das, Carlo Dionisi-Vici, Clara D. van Karnebeek, Julia B. Hennermann, Siobh\'an O'Sullivan, Sabine A. Fuchs, Luciana Hannibal, M. Rebecca Heiner-Fokkema, Marek J. Noga, Irene M. L. W. K\"orver-Keularts, Katja Benedikte Prest{\o} Elgst{\o}en, George J. G. Ruijter, J J M Jans, Amy Harms, Thomas Hankemeier, Maurizio Scarpa, Ines Thiele, Shamima Rahman, Stefan K\"olker, Ronan M. T. Fleming
nominations.abstract: Clinical research in rare diseases is challenged by the limited availability and broad geographical distribution of eligible patients. This necessitates multi-centre collaboration and strategic selection of analytical laboratories based on capacity, cost, and capability. We present a mathematical framework based on cardinality optimisation to support key operational decisions in study design, balancing clinical relevance, feasibility, budgetary constraints, and logistical factors. The framework was implemented in the Reconstruction and Computational Modelling for Inherited Metabolic Diseases (Recon4IMD) project, aiming to recruit 1,900 diagnosed patients across 24 healthcare centres and eight metabolomic laboratories. Compared to both proportional heuristic and greedy marginal allocation baselines, the proposed optimisation model consistently achieved higher recruitment yields in simulated multi-centre scenarios and reduced metabolomic analysis costs by approximately 30% under unconstrained conditions. Notably, both the heuristic and greedy allocation baselines became infeasible under progressively tighter laboratory capacity constraints, whereas the optimised model maintained feasibility and cost control. These findings highlight the value of integrated optimisation strategies for improving recruitment, platform selection, and sample allocation in complex, resource-limited research settings.

nominations.title: Beyond Reconstruction: A Unified Framework for Trustworthy and Explainable EEG Artifact Removal Evaluation
nominations.authors: Phat Lam, Hung Nguyen, Lam Pham, Huy Phan, Dat Tran, Ian McLoughlin, Roozbeh Razavi-Far, Hung Cao
nominations.abstract: Deep-learning methods have achieved strong performance in EEG artifact removal, but evaluation remains dominated by reconstruction metrics such as error, correlation, and signal-to-noise ratio. Although these metrics assess similarity to clean EEG, they do not establish whether models effectively suppress artifacts, preserve neural activity, or provide reliable explanations. To address these limitations, we propose TriX-EEG, a three-level framework for trustworthy and explainable EEG artifact removal. Level 1, Signal Validity (SV), evaluates reconstruction quality and neural band-power preservation. Level 2, Removal Faithfulness (RF), assesses the removed component through artifact error and residual artifact/neural leakage. Level 3, Explanation Reliability (ER), examines model behavior through temporal alignment, causal relevance, and stability. We evaluate TriX-EEG using nine published neural denoisers across three public benchmarks derived from EEGDenoiseNet and the PhysioNet Motion Artifact Contaminated EEG Dataset, covering EOG, EMG, and motion artifacts. Results show that reconstruction metrics alone are insufficient for trustworthy denoiser assessment: RF complements it by revealing whether errors stem from residual artifact or suppressed neural activity, while ER captures distinct aspects of explanation behavior, supporting joint evaluation of three aspects within a unified framework rather than reliance on any single factor. External validation on an independent EEG/EOG dataset and the BCI Competition IV-2a motor-imagery dataset further demonstrates broadly consistent rankings under dataset shift. Higher-ranked denoisers generally preserve more task-relevant information or cause less downstream performance degradation. Overall, TriX-EEG provides a comprehensive basis for EEG denoiser assessment, encouraging models that are not only accurate but also faithful and explainable.

nominations.title: Semantic Communication via Analog RF Computing: When the Radio Computes the Meaning
nominations.authors: Christo Kurisummoottil Thomas
nominations.abstract: Semantic communication (SC) systems transmit continuous latent representations of meaning, but computing the semantic encoder at resource-constrained edge devices incurs substantial energy and memory costs. To address this challenge, we propose an end-to-end SC framework that executes the semantic encoder in the client's RF receiver front end using analog RF computing. A base station (BS) broadcasts encoder weights as RF waveforms, while each edge device reuses its receiver's passive mixer to compute semantic latents at ultra-low energy. These latents are transmitted over the uplink for network-side task inference. We show that analog computing noise across encoder layers and channel noise affecting transmitted latents admit a unified mathematical model. We define a task-posterior semantic distortion metric and derive its second-order decomposition into per-client, per-stage semantic sensitivities. Using this decomposition, we obtain a closed-form semantic-aware water-filling allocation of the total client energy budget across clients, encoder layers, and uplinks, assigning tighter accuracy targets to semantically sensitive stages. This allocation induces a broadcast beamforming problem that accounts for client-specific, per-layer accuracy requirements. We further refine the allocation through stochastic optimization and jointly design it with multi-task noise-aware training of the shared semantic model. MNIST simulations show that, at matched total client energy, the proposed allocation reduces network semantic distortion by 9.2\%-19.2\% compared with uniform precision and 5.1\%-13.1\% compared with client-blind allocation. Noise-aware co-design yields a further 46\% reduction.

nominations.title: Device-Centric Cooperative Floor-Level Estimation under Sparse Anchor Deployment for Construction-Site Applications
nominations.authors: Jiaxu Liang, Zhuoran Li, Osamu Muta, Haruto Morokuma, Naohiro Ikeda, Takamasa Kitanouma
nominations.abstract: For construction-site applications in multi-story buildings, accurate floor-level estimation is important for tracking workers, equipment, and Internet of Things (IoT) devices. In buildings under construction, communication infrastructure and power-supply facilities are often limited and the indoor environment changes as construction progresses, making localization systems that rely on dense wireless infrastructure or fingerprint databases difficult to deploy and maintain. Low-power wide-area (LPWA) communication can provide wide-area coverage with a small number of temporarily deployed access points (APs), but under sparse AP deployment, AP-to-terminal observations alone may provide insufficient floor-related information for reliable floor-level estimation. To address this problem, this paper develops a device-centric cooperative floor-level estimation method that exploits inter-terminal observations as relative floor-difference information to complement AP-side information. For practical application with limited measurement data, AP-to-terminal observations are represented by an upper/lower-AP RSS contrast, while inter-terminal observations are statistically modeled according to floor-difference classes. The resulting AP-side and pairwise scores are combined in a weighted floor-label objective and approximately optimized using dual-order sequential iterated conditional modes (ICM). Ray-tracing simulations and LoRa measurement experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method under different AP deployments and terminal-selection limits.

nominations.title: Hardware Impairment Parameter Estimation in Fluid Antenna Systems by Inverse Optimization
nominations.authors: Songling Zhang, Zhaohui Yang, Ruopeng Xu, Hao Xu, Xusheng Zhu, Zhaoyang Zhang, Kai-Kit Wong
nominations.abstract: In this paper, the problem of estimating the hardware impairment parameters of fluid antennas (FAs) in a multi-base station (BS) multi-user communication system is studied. The actual hardware coefficients are unknown, whereas the FA positions and transmit beamforming vectors adopted by the BSs are known. We first formulate a forward spectral efficiency (SE) maximization problem and introduce aggregate interference variables whose consistency with the physical inter-cell interference can be maintained through a pricing mechanism. For inverse estimation, the aggregate interference is obtained from receiver-side interference measurements associated with the observed network decisions. We then construct a trust-region linear model of the position-update problem around the observed FA positions. To extend the applicability of the proposed framework to antenna positions obtained from inexact or heuristic algorithms, we develop an inverse optimization model with an explicit duality-gap tolerance, which is solved using sequential quadratic programming (SQP). Simulation results show that the proposed scheme attains a lower estimation error than KKT residual minimization (KKT-RM) at both considered transmit-power levels and improves the SE by up to 22.86% over the Ideal-hardware-assumption scheme.

nominations.title: Edge-Combining Subharmonic Mixer-First Receiver
nominations.authors: Eric Danson, Jeffrey S. Walling
nominations.abstract: A 1-10 GHz subharmonic mixer-first receiver using edge combining to drive N-path switches from 50% duty-cycle clocks at half the local oscillator (LO) frequency avoids the gain penalty of harmonic mixing. Inverter-based differential baseband amplifiers with back-gate feedback linearization set their gain by process-defined capacitance ratios, using no additional components and consuming no additional power. A 22 nm fully depleted silicon on insulator (FD-SOI) prototype receiver achieves a conversion gain of 12.8-18.1 dB and a noise figure of 5.7-11 dB across the band. It achieves up to 15.4 dBm out-of-band IIP3 while consuming 16.7-22.3 mW.

nominations.title: Temporal Diffusion Models for Joint Signal-Channel Estimation under Gaussian and $\alpha$-Stable MIMO Channels
nominations.authors: Rawad Kansoh, Bahaa Ammoury, Charbel Hannoun, Jihad Fahs, Ibrahim Abou-Faycal
nominations.abstract: Diffusion models have emerged as powerful tools for learning complex data distributions and solving inverse problems. However, most diffusion models rely on the Gaussian distribution, which does not accurately represent heavy-tailed data. In this work, we study diffusion-based reconstruction under Gaussian and symmetric $\alpha$-stable fading channels, while also exploring the benefits of using possible temporal dependence in the channel. We consider two variants: pilot-based channel-only estimation and joint image-channel recovery for MIMO systems. Our approach is based on several standard and score-based diffusion models for both Gaussian and $\alpha$-stable distributions. We refine these models by guiding the reverse diffusion process using the observation likelihood and show how a single trained diffusion model can be reused for the location-scale family of distributions without retraining. In blind MIMO recovery, separate diffusion models are used for the image and channel, and their estimates are combined through likelihood guidance. For each setting, we compare independent and temporal reconstruction, where information from previous observations is used to improve the estimation. We show that, under a time-dependent channel model, such a temporal reconstruction improves channel estimation and the quality of the reconstructed image. Finally, we show that, for the same heavy-tailed channel data, using an $\alpha$-stable diffusion prior provides better channel estimation and image reconstruction than using a Gaussian diffusion prior.

nominations.title: Least ln-cosh-based adaptive filtering algorithm for graph signal processing
nominations.authors: Chong Zhang, Haiquan Zhao
nominations.abstract: Currently, an increasing number of irregular signals are being defined within graph structures. This paper proposes a Least ln-cosh-based Adaptive Filtering for Graph Signal Processing (GSP LLAF) algorithm for offline/online graph signal estimation under various non-Gaussian noise conditions. Compared to the recently proposed Graph Adaptive Least Mean p-th Power (GSP LMP) algorithm, GSP LLAF eliminates the need for prior knowledge of the noise characteristics. Simultaneously, GSP LLAF addresses the limitation in estimation accuracy encountered by the Sign Algorithm for Graph Signal Processing (GSP Sign) and the Graph Signal Processing algorithm based on the Generalized Maximum Correntropy Criterion (GSP GMCC). Furthermore, the algorithm features low computational complexity and fast execution speed. To achieve a balance between convergence speed and estimation accuracy, a variable step-size variant, the Modified Variable Step-Size Least ln-cosh-based Adaptive Filtering Algorithm for Graph Signal Processing (GSP MVSS-LLAF), is proposed. In estimation experiments involving both static and time-varying graph signals, the proposed GSP LLAF and GSP MVSS-LLAF algorithms demonstrate fast, stable, and robust graph signal estimation performance under various non-Gaussian noise conditions, including Bernoulli-Gaussian (BG) modeled impulse noise, as well as alpha-stable, Cauchy, and Laplace distributions.

nominations.title: Robust DOA Estimation for GNSS-like Signals Under Jamming: A Rotation-Enhanced SWN-MUSIC Approach
nominations.authors: Jiyao Jiang, Xiaowei Cui, Gang Liu, Sihao Zhao, Mingquan Lu
nominations.abstract: In jamming environments, accurate direction-of-arrival (DOA) estimation for Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS)-like signals using antenna arrays is crucial for spoofing detection and subsequent countermeasures. However, estimation accuracy strongly depends on the incident direction of the signal of interest (SOI) under a given jamming and array configuration, with severe errors occurring in certain directions---a phenomenon whose physical mechanisms remain unclear. To address this gap, we identify two types of geometric ill-conditions between the array manifold and the jamming subspace, clarifying that certain directions suffer from inherently unfavorable observation geometry, which cannot be overcome by algorithmic refinement alone. Motivated by this insight, we introduce a paradigm namely rotational diversity, which treats the array attitude as a controllable sensing resource to actively reconfigure the observation geometry, thereby providing complementary perspectives in which the problematic directions can be accurately estimated. To implement this paradigm, we develop a Rotation-Enhanced Spatial Whitening and Normalized Multiple Signal Classification (SWN-MUSIC) framework, which performs independent DOA estimations across multiple rotation angles and selectively integrates reliable estimates. Simulation results demonstrate substantial improvement in accuracy in the directions that were poorly estimated under the fixed-array SWN-MUSIC, while maintaining performance in well-conditioned directions, thereby producing more robust DOA estimates.

nominations.title: Reference Coordinates, Output Perturbations, and Information Loss in EEG Decoding
nominations.authors: Runni Zhou, Rongrong Fu, Xinghao Yan, Xiaoyang Li
nominations.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) decoders can respond to reference changes that preserve all relative-potential information. We use established measurement-operator theory to distinguish coordinate sensitivity, additional output-channel perturbations, and electrode loss. Exact pseudoinverse alignment supplies a consistency control; measurement-operator canonicalization (MOC) denotes a graph-Tikhonov estimator. The broader evaluation covers three public motor-imagery datasets and four decoders. The primary EEGNet comparison on Cho2017 and PhysioNet uses three paired training seeds, three shared noise realizations, and six front ends, with identical CAR training inputs sharing checkpoints. At 10 dB output perturbation, MOC-minus-raw disagreement was -0.144 and -0.107, while balanced-accuracy differences were 0.044 and 0.050, respectively; these four contrasts passed the retained Holm correction. MOC also reduced disagreement relative to pseudoinversion across all three seeds in both cohorts. However, comparison with fixed graph smoothing after pseudoinversion did not establish an additional MOC benefit. Preserving zero reference rows changed raw disagreement by less than 0.001 in magnitude; inverse-method predictions were unchanged. For canonical front ends, cross-reference disagreement was close to the reference obtained from independent noise within the same operator. Controlled weak-mode reconstruction and equal-rank electrode masks exposed separate stability and information-loss effects. The results locate the complete-reference gains within spatial processing under the specified stress model, while requiring decoding accuracy alongside consistency to assess practical utility.

nominations.title: Structured Design of Layered Sparse Unitary Space-Time Modulation for Integrated Noncoherent and Coherent MIMO Communications
nominations.authors: \'{A}lvaro Pend\'{a}s-Recondo, Enrique Pend\'{a}s-Recondo, Rafael Gonz\'{a}lez Ayestar\'{a}n, Jes\'{u}s Alberto L\'{o}pez-Fern\'{a}ndez, Ignacio Santamaria
nominations.abstract: This work presents a novel structured constellation design based on unitary space-time modulation (USTM) for integrated noncoherent and coherent multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) communications. Information is encoded into the sparse space-time matrices through two layers: a noncoherent layer that distinguishes points on the Grassmann manifold (subspaces) and a coherent layer that distinguishes among the Stiefel representatives associated with each of those points (bases for the subspaces). We consider sequential decoding of the two layers to reduce computational complexity, while explicitly identifying the matrix structures that favor this decoding strategy. The proposed constellation builds on a previous structured Grassmannian signaling design, which has the remarkable property of producing space-time matrices with a single nonzero entry per row, while introducing a novel systematic design for the second layer corresponding to the Stiefel representatives. The design of the second layer preserves the sparsity of the first layer and significantly reduces the decoding computational complexity, while ensuring reliable performance under sequential decoding and enabling a simple yet effective bit labeling, as validated by numerical results in terms of bit error rate (BER) and symbol error rate (SER). Numerical results also show graceful performance degradation under channel correlation and, for limited coherence intervals where channel state information at the receiver (CSIR) can be estimated only imperfectly, improved performance compared with classical space-time block coding (STBC) schemes based on QAM and PSK.

nominations.title: Generation of Sample Complex Wishart Distributed Matrices and Change Detection in Polarimetric SAR Data
nominations.authors: Allan A. Nielsen, Henning Skriver, Knut Conradsen
nominations.abstract: The complex Wishart distribution is used to describe synthetic aperture radar (SAR) data in the so-called covariance matrix representation. We give a test statistic for detection of differences between two instances in this distribution and an associated probability measure. Generated complex Wishart distributed covariance matrices are used to show that this test statistic and the probability measure in situations with no differences follow the expected distributions.

nominations.title: Distributed Blind Source Separation from Compressed Mixtures
nominations.authors: Amir Weiss
nominations.abstract: Blind source separation (BSS) is increasingly needed in sensing architectures where mixtures are acquired by multiple remote devices but the inference itself is carried out centrally. In such systems, the sensors often cannot transmit their raw observations since the communication links are rate-limited, energy-limited, or both. The fusion center therefore must recover the latent sources from compressed versions of the mixtures. This setting raises questions that classical BSS models do not address directly: whether source identifiability survives compression, how separation accuracy changes under a specified compression model, and how the separation procedure should be modified to account for the statistical model induced by the compression stage. In this work, we develop a framework for distributed BSS from compressed mixtures that addresses these issues at three levels. First, we formalize identifiability under compression and establish a data-processing viewpoint showing that compression cannot introduce distinguishability that is absent before compression. Second, for mixtures of Gaussian sources with general covariance structures, we derive an idealized Gaussian rate-distortion-based Cram\'er-Rao lower bound benchmark for the interference-to-source ratio. Third, we develop practical compression-aware separation schemes based on subtractively dithered quantization together with debiasing at the fusion center for both fourth-order-cumulant-based and second-order-statistics-based methods. Simulation experiments demonstrate the resulting tradeoffs between communication rate and separation performance and the gains obtained by compression-aware separation in representative distributed sensing scenarios.

nominations.title: StreamingDPD: A 1.28-GSa/s Instantaneous-Power-Gated Depthwise TCN Accelerator for Real-Time 320-MHz Digital Predistortion
nominations.authors: Yizhuo Wu, Xinling Wang, Chang Gao
nominations.abstract: State feedback between successive samples limits the streaming throughput of recurrent neural networks for digital predistortion (DPD). We present StreamingDPD, an accelerator that processes 320-MHz signals at 1.28 GSa/s. Its 207-parameter instantaneous-power-gated depthwise temporal convolutional network (IPG-DWTCN) uses $|x[n]|^2$ to gate feature channels and causal dilated depthwise convolutions to model power amplifier memory. The network maps to a spatially unrolled fixed-point pipeline with shift-based quadratic activations and layer-wise mixed precision, sustaining one complex sample per cycle per lane. Its algorithmic cost is 554 floating-point operations per complex sample, 30.1% fewer than the recurrent baseline with the best linearization performance. In RF playback measurements on three power amplifiers driven by 40- to 320-MHz Wi-Fi 6/7 and 5G NR waveforms, IPG-DWTCN achieves the lowest mean adjacent-channel power ratio (ACPR) and ranks first or ties for first in mean error vector magnitude (EVM) against five neural baselines of comparable size. Four-lane FPGA hardware-in-the-loop tests on a 320-MHz 4096-QAM Wi-Fi 7 waveform achieve -45.82 dBc ACPR and -42.94 dB EVM at 1.28 GSa/s. At the same sample rate, post-layout evaluation of a single-lane 12-nm FinFET ASIC yields a 0.10 mm$^2$ core, a 52-cycle (40.63 ns) latency, and an estimated typical-corner power of 142.21 mW (111.10 pJ/sample). Relative to the prior 22-nm recurrent DPD ASIC, the design provides 5.1 times the throughput at about one-seventh the energy per sample.

nominations.title: Remark on internal relaxation in large number qubit systems
nominations.authors: Martin Jan{\ss}en
nominations.abstract: For a time $t_{c}$ of calculation in an $N$ qubit quantum computer that is much shorter than the intrinsic Heisenberg time $t_H$, $t_c\ll t_H$, the dynamics of the system is effectively irreversible and the couplings between the qubits give rise to a relaxation time scale $\tau_r$. If $t_H\gg t_c >\sim \tau_r$ one looses quantum coherence exponentially fast. Since $t_H$ scales exponentially with $N$ there is a threshold $N_c$ such that for $N\gg N_c$ one must be aware of possible intrinsic relaxation during calculation. As an order of magnitude estimation we find $N_c\approx \ln(\tau_r/T)$ where $T$ is a typical system specific oscillation time of a single qubit. $\tau_r$ can be estimated as the typical inverse transition rate between two parts of the system, one of which is treated as an environment of the other.

nominations.title: CSS circuits are ICM circuits without magic states
nominations.authors: Alexandru Paler
nominations.abstract: Gidney and Jones recently introduced ``CSS circuits'', generated by $X$, $Z$, $\MX$, $\MZ$ and CNOT, and showed that they can be sampled with $O(1)$ work per gate. They suspected that the class had been seen before. We point out that it is, up to a normal form, the initialisation--CNOT--measurement (ICM) form introduced in 2015 for compiling fault-tolerant circuits, restricted to $\ket{0}$ and $\ket{+}$ initialisations. The ICM construction answers constructively their question about ``non-CSS-ness as a resource'': every Clifford$+T$ circuit compiles to a CSS circuit acting on $\ket{Y}$ and $\ket{A}$ input states.

nominations.title: QEDist: Practical Exact Distance Certification for Stabilizer Codes
nominations.authors: Jong Yeon Lee
nominations.abstract: We present QEDist, a method and software package that certifies the distance of qubit stabilizer codes. Building on tree-search methods, QEDist constructs candidate logical operators one qubit at a time, using sparse parity checks, stabilizer equivalence, and verified symmetries to reduce the work. For a cutoff $W$, a completed search either finds a nontrivial logical operator of weight at most $W$ or proves that none exists. Because satisfying one check can violate another, we use both satisfied and unsatisfied checks to lower-bound the weight needed to complete a logical operator, and prune branches whose bound exceeds the remaining budget, which substantially reduces net search time. We benchmark QEDist mainly on Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) codes; the same formulation extends to non-CSS codes and to the fault distance of syndrome-extraction circuits. For lifted-product (LP) codes, we further exploit the product structure to replace part of the full-code search with a smaller search on a classical constituent. We establish exact distances for codes with up to several thousand qubits, including Abelian and non-Abelian LP codes whose distances were previously reported only as upper bounds. In several seconds of search on one laptop core, QEDist certifies exact distances up to 20 for many of these codes and fault distance 10 for the syndrome-extraction circuit of the $[[144,12,12]]$ code. With orders-of-magnitude speedups over the tested exact solvers, QEDist makes exact distance certification a practical tool for selecting and optimizing finite-length quantum codes.

nominations.title: Black holes as black boxes: a query lower bound on python's lunch decoding
nominations.authors: Chris Waddell, Michelle Xu
nominations.abstract: The python's lunch conjecture relates the complexity of bulk reconstruction in holographic tensor networks to an exponential cost associated with post-selection. We establish a tight query lower bound for this decoding problem in a Haar random oracle model, with a python's lunch circuit that applies Haar random unitary $U$ to a logical input and fixed ancillas, followed by post-selection on $m$ output qubits. Given one copy of the normalized encoded state and coherent oracle access to $U$ and $U^\dagger$, including controlled queries, we prove that recovering even a single logical bit with constant average advantage requires $\Omega(2^{m/2})$ queries. Together with the state-independent amplitude amplification upper bound for approximately isometric encodings, this establishes query complexity $\Theta(2^{m/2})$ at constant decoding accuracy. We also comment on the decoding cost for other "admissible'" ensembles of unitaries $U$ which give rise to families of approximately isometric holographic maps.

nominations.title: A Proposal for Quantum Reference Frames in Quantum Field Theory and their Experimental Exploration
nominations.authors: Ivan Agullo, Fabio M. Mele
nominations.abstract: We construct quantum reference frames (QRFs) in quantum field theory, using localized modes of a scalar field as frames for its shift symmetry. We import tools from relativistic quantum information to explicitly compute entropies and correlation measures of relational observables, investigating their frame dependence and the new features arising from the field-theoretic character of the system. Unlike QRFs for systems with finitely many degrees of freedom, localized field-theoretic QRFs are necessarily mixed in physically relevant states and generically correlated with the subsystems they describe. These aspects of QRFs for fields affect the properties of relational observables in a subtle way. Furthermore, we put forward a proposal for testing these predictions with existing quantum simulators based on ultracold atoms and quantum fluids, thus connecting QRF physics with analogue gravity platforms.

nominations.title: Restoring quantum neural network trainability through reusable calibration
nominations.authors: Ruizhe Shen, Xianquan Yan, Kenji Kawaguchi, Ching Hua Lee
nominations.abstract: Quantum neural networks (QNNs) rely on measured quantum observables to guide optimization, but hardware noise can suppress the parameter-dependent signals essential for learning. Here, we develop a structure-preserving error-mitigation framework that improves QNN trainability through reusable calibration of the quantum circuit's effective noise response. By calibrating a reference circuit with the same gate architecture as the trainable circuit, we construct regularized estimators of local quantum features that remain fixed throughout training. We quantify how calibration errors and response mismatches affect the recovery of both observables and their derivatives. Numerical simulations demonstrate enhanced loss-landscape contrast, faster convergence, and improved classification performance, and an IBM Quantum experiment confirms improved closed-loop variational optimization under hardware noise. We further demonstrate calibration reuse in a modular QNN comprising 25 independent four-qubit channels, corresponding to 100 qubits in aggregate. Our results establish reusable feature calibration as a practical approach to improving noise-limited quantum machine learning without repeated calibration at every training step.

nominations.title: Robust Passive Quantum Memory in Three Dimensions, Part I: Thermal and Zero-Temperature Perturbative Stability
nominations.authors: Patrick Hayden
nominations.abstract: Whether a three-dimensional quantum many-body system with geometrically local, bounded-degree interactions can passively protect encoded quantum information has remained a central open question since Kitaev introduced topological quantum computation. Passive protection requires stability against both thermal noise at nonzero temperature and generic static Hamiltonian perturbations Balasubramanian, Davydova, and Lin (BDL) recently established unperturbed three-dimensional thermal self-correction using a recursively defined family of stabilizer Hamiltonians. However, they left open whether their construction remains stable against quantum perturbations, even at zero temperature. In this paper, we show that a slight variant of the BDL code family achieves stability along both boundary axes of the perturbation-temperature phase diagram as the system size grows. Following BDL, in the absence of perturbation it is thermally stable below a critical temperature, achieving a stretched-exponentially long memory lifetime when coupled to any local Markovian thermal bath generated by single-site system-bath interactions satisfying detailed balance with bounded coupling rates. At zero temperature under arbitrary weak, superpolynomially decaying quantum perturbations, the family maintains a uniform bulk spectral gap, superpolynomially small ground-space splitting, and a superpolynomially long closed-system unitary memory lifetime for quasi-locally dressed logical observables. To prove this zero-temperature stability, we establish local topological quantum order across the multiscale hierarchy using a linearly dilated relaxation of the usual Bravyi-Hastings-Michalakis criteria. In the companion paper, we combine the tools developed here with finite-temperature worldline cluster expansions to establish passive self-correction throughout the phase diagram's positive-temperature perturbed interior.

nominations.title: Loss-Tolerant Quantum Correlations Between Atomic and Photonic Qubits
nominations.authors: Leonardo Ruscio, Love A. Pettersson, Philip Thomas, Stefano Paesani, Olivier Morin, Anders S. S{\o}rensen, Gerhard Rempe
nominations.abstract: Quantum physics forbids cloning of a qubit. Therefore, a qubit is irreversibly lost upon loss of the information carrier. To mitigate this physical loss, it has been proposed to distribute the logical information across an entangled set of physical qubits, some of which can be lost. Previous experiments illustrated this concept, but failed to demonstrate a gain in the information-retrieval efficiency. Here we address this challenge with photons for which the total loss, from generation to detection, is below the loss-tolerance threshold of $50\%$. Using two single-atom emitters in an optical cavity, we encode information into the photons of a graph state and observe an efficiency gain for retrieving quantum correlations between the atoms and the photons for single-qubit measurements in the Pauli $X$ and $Z$ bases. Although technical errors reduce the probability to obtain the \textit{correct} result, we achieve average fidelities as high as $\gtrsim\!70\%$ without and $\gtrsim\!75\%$ with error detection, demonstrating entanglement between the atomic and encoded photonic qubits. Lowering the encoding errors is a next natural step toward loss-tolerant photonic quantum-information processing.

nominations.title: Distrustful entanglement-based Quantum Key Distribution
nominations.authors: Shubhayan Sarkar
nominations.abstract: Quantum key distribution (QKD) is the one of the most explored application of quantum information theory. While practical QKD systems are being deployed around the world, a major issue of these setups are that one has to trust the measurement devices of both parties. On the other hand, the most secure among such schemes are called device-independent (DI) QKD protocols, where no component of the setup is assumed to be trusted. However, due to their high technological demand, their loophole-free version currently remain out of practical reach. Inspired by the real world, we consider the traditional QKD in a distrustful measurement setting, that is, the measurement devices can only be trusted upto some level of confidence, which might still be large but not completely trusted. We then derive a general lower bound on the asymptotic key rate in this scenario. Then considering perfect detectors and source, and the entanglement-based BB84 (BBM) protocol, we show that to obtain secure keys one needs to trust their devices more than 82 %. However, we observe that such a protocol can not be realised with any level of distrust using the realistic detectors and sources at the current technology. Finally, we also consider the BBM protocol with arbitrary dimensional systems and observe that they are more robust to distrust than qubit systems. Consequently, with the same level of distrust, along with same detector and source efficiences, one can get better key rates with high-dimensional systems.

nominations.title: AI Scientist Discovered Robust Quantum Control
nominations.authors: Jiahao Yan, Xuanying Lai, Xiaoshui Lin, Yizhou Wang, Changyu Yao, Guanghui He, Thomas Lewer, Chong Zu, Chuanwei Zhang
nominations.abstract: Protecting quantum coherence is a central theme of modern quantum technologies. Carefully designed control pulses can extend coherence by suppressing disorder and unwanted interactions. However, designing robust pulse sequences remains challenging in interacting multi-level systems, where multiple independent error channels must be controlled in the presence of experimental imperfections. Here we introduce QORA, a multi-agent artificial intelligence framework that integrates theoretical reasoning, automated experimental calibration and control for closed-loop discovery of quantum control sequences. Applied to a dense ensemble of spin-1 nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond, QORA discovers AID-ROD, a series of AI-discovered sequences that nearly double the measured spin coherence time relative to the state-of-the-art human-designed sequence DROID-C3PO. Subsequence analysis by human researchers reveals a hierarchy of error suppression: 18-pulse blocks suppress linear and quadratic onsite disorder and common-mode drive-amplitude errors, while their arrangement over a longer cycle reduces dipolar interactions, providing a physical explanation for the observed improvement and robustness in AID-ROD. These results demonstrate AI-guided experimental discovery of robust quantum control and identify a design strategy for protecting coherence in interacting multi-level systems beyond qubits.

nominations.title: Quantum Reference Frames, Locality, and Microcausality in Quantum Field Theory
nominations.authors: Christopher J. Fewster, Leon Loveridge
nominations.abstract: As a consequence of the relativistic spectrum condition, quantum reference frames for translations on Minkowski space are never described by projection-valued measures, and in many cases fail a weaker spacetime localisation property known as the norm-$1$ condition. This has several implications for the local and observable structure of quantum field theories described relative to even the best available frame: for a large class of frame states, strict locality is replaced by almost locality, and microcausality by commutators that decay rapidly with increasing separation, corresponding to an effective smearing of the light cone by the localisation density of the frame state. Operations built from finitely many almost local Kraus operators, for example nonselective measurements of relativised local observables, satisfy an approximate no-signalling bound, with a residue attributable to the localisation uncertainty of the frame. Whether causality in its strongest operational form -- non-disturbance under all physically realisable operations -- survives relativisation is left open.
