An upshot of our finding is that quantum field theories formulated relative to a quantum reference frame cannot rest on the traditional axioms, and some general relational axiomatisation must replace at least some of them by taking into account physically realistic properties of the frame.

nominations.title: Transient State Preservation of a Dissipative Qubit via Lyapunov Control
nominations.authors: Ilan Sabaj, Pablo Monz\'on
nominations.abstract: Preserving quantum states in the presence of environmental decoherence remains a fundamental challenge for quantum information processing. This work investigates whether Hamiltonian Lyapunov feedback can transiently preserve the state of an open qubit by reshaping its trajectory under Markovian dissipation. A state-error Lyapunov function is adopted to derive an analytical feedback law for Lindblad dynamics, ensuring a nonincreasing Lyapunov function whenever the control sensitivities are nonzero. The analysis identifies the geometric conditions under which the feedback becomes ineffective, showing that control authority vanishes when the current and target Bloch vectors are collinear. Numerical simulations are performed for amplitude damping and pure dephasing using selected target states. Performance is evaluated through fidelity, accumulated infidelity, dwell time above a fidelity threshold, coherence, and control effort. The results demonstrate that the proposed feedback cannot eliminate irreversible dissipation or achieve universal asymptotic stabilization, but it can provide transient benefits for selected target-channel combinations. In particular, under amplitude damping, the controller significantly reduces accumulated infidelity and substantially extends the interval during which the system remains above a prescribed fidelity threshold. In the pure dephasing cases examined, improvements in fidelity are generally limited, although transient coherence preservation is observed for the oblique target considered, revealing a trade-off between coherence and state fidelity. These findings indicate that Lyapunov-based Hamiltonian feedback is best suited as a transient preservation mechanism and motivate its application to gate operations and preservation of prepared states during finite time intervals before their use or readout.

nominations.title: Microwave-optical quantum transduction with quantum-well exciton polaritons
nominations.authors: Nicholas S. Yama, Mohammad Khalifa, Yuxuan Wei, Adbhut Gupta, Loren N. Pfeiffer, Feng Wang, Alp Sipahigil
nominations.abstract: Linking superconducting quantum processors over optical fiber requires microwave-optical quantum transducers that are efficient, high-bandwidth, and low-noise. This combination has been out of reach because of the weak nonlinearities of conventional electro-optic (EO) materials. We propose a transducer with an engineered, strong EO nonlinearity using the quantum-confined Stark effect (QCSE) of quantum-well excitons. The QCSE transducer leverages the strong light-matter interactions and extreme polarizability of quantum well excitons. Strong coupling to an optical cavity forms exciton-polaritons whose vacuum EO coupling is up to five orders of magnitude larger than in a typical thin-film lithium niobate device. We describe a GaAs/AlGaAs stepped-quantum-well transducer design with predicted transduction efficiencies above 60% and fewer than 0.01 added noise quanta over a $\sim$60 MHz bandwidth, using pump powers below 10 $\mu$W and loaded optical and microwave quality factors of only $3\times10^4$ and $10^3$. We further show that the cavity protection of the polariton provides robustness against inhomogeneous broadening of the quantum well excitons.

nominations.title: Charge self-consistent DFT+QDMFT framework with a Krylov-based quantum impurity solver
nominations.authors: M. Karabin, T. Sohail, E. A. Coello P\'erez, S. Ghosh, M. Sajjan, H. Terletska, M. Eisenbach
nominations.abstract: We integrate a quantum impurity solver into a charge self-consistent density functional theory (DFT) plus quantum dynamical mean-field theory framework. The solver optimizes adaptive circuits to approximate the ground state of the impurity model and its particle and hole excitations, and reconstructs the impurity Green's function from their Hamiltonian moments. Higher-order moments are predicted from low-order ones using a machine-learning model, while regularized optimization mitigates violations of causality in the resulting self-energy. The latter is used to update the charge density until self-consistency is achieved. We demonstrate the framework through body-centered cubic lithium calculations and compare the results with a reference one using a continuous-time quantum Monte Carlo solver. These calculations converge with root-mean-square charge-density residuals below $\boldsymbol{2\times10^{-3}}$ and yield a nearly vanishing impurity self-energy, consistent with the noninteracting limit used for weakly correlated lithium.

nominations.title: Infrared fluctuations and collective entanglement modes in harmonic lattices
nominations.authors: Mahsa Lezgi, Ali Mollabashi
nominations.abstract: We investigate how infrared fluctuations and spatial separation shape vacuum entanglement between two finite regions in the relativistic harmonic chain and its Lifshitz generalizations. At fixed lattice spacing and finite geometry, we establish that logarithmic negativity remains uniformly bounded as the mass approaches zero, while mutual information diverges. Infrared-enhanced total correlations therefore do not provide an unbounded distillable-entanglement resource. Using local symplectic consolidation, we identify the collective canonical modes carrying the negativity and follow their evolution with separation. Their participation crosses over from localization near the facing boundaries to a collective distribution within each region. Expansion in the adjacent-state canonical basis connects this evolution to progressively weaker, more extended reference modes, including adjacent-halo directions. Building on the established concentration of long-distance logarithmic negativity into a single canonical pair, we show that its spatial participation is smooth and infrared-dominated despite its ultraviolet canonical structure, a distinction also present in pure-state entanglement modes. These results refine the ultraviolet mode picture by resolving the long-wavelength organization of the oscillators participating in the surviving entanglement. Across the massless dispersions studied, the normalized participation approaches a universal long-distance profile when separation is scaled by the negativity radius. Its detailed form and the entanglement range nevertheless remain sensitive to ultraviolet deformations. Together, these findings distinguish infrared-enhanced correlations from distillable entanglement and reveal the collective spatial organization underlying its persistence at large separation.

nominations.title: Quantum-Classical Separation in Probability Distribution Transport via Nonlocal Games
nominations.authors: Fangjun Hu, Xun Gao
nominations.abstract: In many-body physics and generative artificial intelligence, locality provides a natural notion of phase equivalence: two quantum states or classical probability distributions are regarded as in the same phase when local dynamics can reversibly transform one into the other. This raises a fundamental question: can local quantum dynamics transport classical probability distributions in ways that local classical dynamics cannot? We establish a quantum-classical separation in distribution transport: two classical distributions can be connected exactly and reversibly by a constant-depth local quantum circuit, whereas classical stochastic transport requires a substantially larger spatial range. We demonstrate this separation explicitly on a one-dimensional chain and develop a general construction principle on graphs, based on nonlocal games. Moreover, the source distribution can itself be generated by a simple local classical process, establishing a quantum advantage in distribution generation as well. Our results reveal a fundamental distinction between classical and quantum local reversibility, even when both the initial and final states are entirely classical.

nominations.title: Quantum Fisher information matrices for time-evolved bosonic Gaussian thermal states
nominations.authors: Hailey S. Murray, Diego Estrada, Mark M. Wilde
nominations.abstract: Quantum Fisher information (QFI) is a fundamental quantum metrological quantity arising from the second order term in a Taylor expansion of a smooth divergence evaluated at nearby quantum states. The $\alpha$-$z$ information matrix is a QFI measure arising from the $\alpha$-$z$ R\'enyi relative entropy, and QFI measures corresponding to various underlying smooth divergences may be recovered from the $\alpha$-$z$ information matrix, including the standard symmetric logarithmic derivative (SLD) QFI. Bosonic Gaussian states are common probe states for quantum metrological tasks and admit a complete characterization in terms of their first and second moments. In this work, we consider the quantum metrological task of estimating parameters that characterize a Gaussian unitary time evolution of a faithful bosonic Gaussian thermal state. We establish a formula for the $\alpha$-$z$ information matrix of faithful bosonic Gaussian thermal states that have undergone a Gaussian unitary time evolution. As an example, we calculate entries of the $\alpha$-$z$ information matrix for a two-mode Gaussian thermal state that has undergone a beam splitting operation. For a parametrized family of time-evolved bosonic Gaussian states, we also derive a formula for the SLD operator, which is known to provide a measurement scheme that saturates the quantum Cr\'amer-Rao bound and thus achieves the ultimate precision for single parameter estimation.

nominations.title: A Geometric Framework for Local-to-Global Symmetry: Global Constraints on Local Dynamics
nominations.authors: Connor Terry Weatherly, Roel Tempelaar
nominations.abstract: Aggregate molecular systems are routinely understood by decomposing them into local structural units, such as monomers in J/H-aggregates, chemical moieties, motifs, and functional groups. Implicit in such decompositions is the assumption that these local structures remain meaningful within the aggregate. Here, we ask how the symmetries of constituent structures relate to aggregate symmetry, and how this relation determines the constraints that global symmetry imposes on transitions between local symmetry sectors. We construct a covariant local-to-global representation from framed local symmetry data and show that its reconstruction map intertwines with a global quantum representation. By identifying which global symmetry sectors overlap each local symmetry sector, we resolve symmetry-enforced dynamical exclusions into site-resolved pathways. Through Frobenius reciprocity, these exclusions can be determined from standard character tables of the local and global symmetry groups, with the character values in the inner product paired according to the relative positions and orientations of local structures within the aggregate. Although motivated by molecular aggregates, the construction is formulated for arbitrary geometries modeled by a homogeneous space of an ambient transformation group.

nominations.title: Probing the real-time decoding accuracy bounds in trapped ion architectures
nominations.authors: Arianna Meinking, Evangelia Takou, Kenneth R. Brown
nominations.abstract: Fault tolerant quantum computers will rely on real-time decoders that process syndromes faster than the QEC cycle duration. The millisecond cycle times offered by trapped ion platforms relax low-latency decoding demands, but simulations and experiments have not yet exploited this time budget to reach maximum logical error suppression. We show how a hybrid sliding window decoding scheme composed of a lower-accuracy and a higher-accuracy decoder can yield substantially improved logical error rates, while preserving low latency. All windows are handled by the lower-accuracy decoder, with some windows being infrequently switched to the higher-accuracy decoder. We extract soft-output information from the lower-accuracy decoder efficiently for any QLDPC code, which allows us to identify decoding windows of low confidence. We simulate memory experiments of bivariate bicycle (BB) codes, using trapped-ion informed noise models. Depending on the physical error rate and BB code, we find up to 3-4 orders of magnitude logical error rate reduction compared to the $\texttt{BP-LSD}$ decoder, and up to 2-3 orders of magnitude lower logical error rate compared to the $\texttt{Beamsearch}$ decoder. By leveraging available classical processing time, our decoding protocol significantly boosts decoding accuracy, ultimately reducing the demands on increasing code size.

nominations.title: Simplifying models of noisy stabilizer QEC on leakage qubits by Pauli twirling
nominations.authors: Alex Kwiatkowski, Aaron J. Friedman
nominations.abstract: The growing capabilities of quantum error-correction (QEC) experiments make it increasingly important to develop methods that predict or assess logical performance over many QEC cycles. Prior work has shown that a stabilizer QEC cycle subject to Pauli-stochastic noise can be modeled by a classical Markov process over syndrome states, with a logical Pauli channel attached to each syndrome transition. Here, we extend this framework to systems in which physical qubits are subject to leakage. We first develop the theory of leakage-dephased Pauli twirling and show that twirled processes can be expressed in terms of Pauli maps on the computational subspace, conditioned on transitions between leakage patterns. We apply this theory to noisy stabilizer QEC with leakage, demonstrating that a QEC cycle with leakage can be modeled by a classical Markov process over the joint syndrome and leakage patterns, with a logical Pauli channel attached to each joint transition. Finally, we derive a transfer-matrix description of repeated QEC cycles and an exact transfer-matrix expression for the success probability of a QEC memory experiment. This framework connects leaky error models of the individual components of the QEC cycle to many-cycle logical performance and provides a foundation for logical characterization and benchmarking methods that can account for leakage.

nominations.title: A Critical Appraisal and Motivated Intruder Test of A Search Dataset Anonymised for the Purposes of the EU Digital Markets Act
nominations.authors: Ghislain d'Entremont, Lisa Pilgram, Sophie Stalla-Bourdillon, Renee Gil, Lucy Mosquera, Olga Vovk, Khaled El Emam
nominations.abstract: This study evaluated the European Commission's anonymisation measures for Alphabet's search-data sharing under Article 6(11) of the Digital Markets Act against European Data Protection Board guidance and contemporary practice, and assessed re-identification through motivated intruder testing. The measures focus on search end-users, leaving other individuals mentioned in queries insufficiently protected, and do not explicitly address inference. The accompanying controls and safeguards reflect good practice for managing residual risk. Motivated intruder testing targeted 98,501 individuals across six countries using publicly available profiles. Google-verified matches yielded a re-identification rate of 0.094%, below the study's 0.47% per-team threshold. Each verified match required about three hours (Euro 105), excluding Google verification and Gemini costs, suggesting limited cost deterrence. All country-level rates were below the threshold, but one region exceeded it. The threshold drew on conservative precedents, adjusted for data quality, verification, controls and safeguards, assuming five independent attack teams. Some sensitivity scenarios exceeded the threshold, but relied on strong assumptions, such as treating all uncertain matches as correct. Results may not generalise beyond the targeted population, and ethics requirements constrained the attacks. Personal data detection recall was assumed rather than tested: the minimum defensible recall was 0.88, with 0.976 recommended. However, missed identifiers outside the allow-list would remain in the dataset. Under the study's contextual framework, assumptions and testing limitations, identity-disclosure risk was considered insignificant. This finding does not resolve the gaps concerning inference and other individuals' information; safeguards remain necessary.

nominations.title: Stop Early, Stay Simple: Evidence Acquisition for Power System Fault and Attack Diagnosis
nominations.authors: S M Zia Ur Rashid, Sazidul Islam Hira, Rupesh Sah, Suman Rath
nominations.abstract: Diagnostic models for cyber-physical power systems usually inspect every telemetry source for every event, although some events are clear from one source and others need several. We ask when a learned policy for choosing that evidence is worth its added complexity. To answer this, we present ActiGrid, a benchmark framework for active evidence acquisition that pairs a classifier trained to tolerate missing modalities with a Double Deep Q-Network (DQN), which either requests another source or stops and diagnoses but never operates grid actuators. On the public TU Delft digital substation and MSU/ORNL power system attack benchmarks, we compare the DQN with fixed subsets and orders, calibrated entropy stopping, a greedy value of information rule, and tree ensembles trained per subset. The learned policy does adapt to what it observes, yet it is statistically indistinguishable from entropy stopping on TU Delft and Pareto dominated by simple controls on MSU/ORNL, while compact subset classifiers outperform it while reading fewer sources on both benchmarks. Entropy stopping run over those subset classifiers reaches the highest mean Macro-F1 on TU Delft (0.928 while reading 57% of the sources) but brings no saving over a static three source subset on MSU/ORNL, where no method exceeds 0.45 Macro-F1. Selective acquisition can pay off, but on these benchmarks it does not need a learned policy.

nominations.title: Watermark Evidence under Open-Weight LLM Modification: Exact Bounds for Low-Rank Output Watermarks
nominations.authors: Prashant Shekhar, Dumindu Samaraweera, Caroline Howard
nominations.abstract: Open-weight language models can continue generating after their released weights are modified, while a watermark verifier still scores outputs against the original base and marked models. We study how such modifications change the evidence available to an OpenStamp-style verifier. At each shared prefix, we represent the modification as a residual in the next-token logits. We derive an exact finite-vocabulary lower bound on the expected log-likelihood-ratio evidence under a residual-span constraint, along with a sharp span-only deviation bound. We also characterize the first-order evidence shift through a covariance term with an explicit second-order remainder, and determine the residual span needed to reach a target evidence level. For sequence-level detection, we derive an exact conditional exponential-moment bound and combine it with a supermartingale argument and a distribution-free order-statistic tolerance bound. This yields a high-confidence upper bound on miss probability after attack selection on calibration data and evaluation on independent certification continuations. In experiments with OpenStamp on Llama-2-7B and Mistral-7B-v0.3, INT8 quantization and 30% pruning retain test true-positive rates of 85.6-94.8%, while 500-step LoRA fine-tuning lowers them to 28.8% and 11.6%. The covariance prediction tracks the measured mean LoRA evidence drift on both models, with no remainder-bound violations across 160,000 test prefixes. Additionally, we observe zero false positives among 500 base-model continuations per model. Through these theoretical and empirical results, the current research provides a better understanding of watermark robustness to model-editing/tuning attacks.

nominations.title: LLMs as Validators for Cross-Chain Bridges: Evaluating Source-Level and Transaction-Level Attack Detection on Solana
nominations.authors: Yasir Rahman, Ishraq Samiha, Shahnewaz Karim Sakib, Anindya Bijoy Das
nominations.abstract: Cross-chain bridges have suffered substantial asset losses due to vulnerabilities in their on-chain programs. On Solana, missing validation checks can enable exploits even when the underlying blockchain operates correctly. The ability of large language models (LLMs) to diagnose these flaws from source code or transaction records, rather than merely raise alarms, remains insufficiently understood. We implement a native Rust lock-and-mint bridge on a local Solana validator with four exploitable variants: two model flaws from the Cashio and Wormhole incidents, while the other two represent vulnerability classes documented in Solana security audits. Paired vulnerable and secure programs, together with successful attacks, benign sessions, and blocked attempts, allow us to distinguish correct diagnoses from unsupported alarms. We evaluate six configurations of five open-weight models across 16,800 responses, compare source inputs with and without comments, and grade 7,200 answers on vulnerable inputs using two blinded LLM graders. The results reveal substantial differences across conditions: without comments, models diagnose 24% of vulnerable source inputs while frequently flagging the secure bridge. Transaction diagnosis is high for the missing-signer scenario but averages 6% across the other three scenarios. Original comments, some of which describe the flaw, increase source diagnosis to 60%. These findings highlight the importance of distinguishing correct vulnerability diagnoses from unsupported alarms in bridge security review.

nominations.title: Threat Landscape of Vibe Coding and the Road to Secure Autonomy
nominations.authors: Devki Nandan Jha, Shubh Anand, Karthick Keeranagere Krishnaiah, Roman Ahearn, Suhas Nale
nominations.abstract: Vibe coding is reshaping software development, enabling faster implementation and allowing individuals with limited programming experience to describe requirements in natural language while AI agents write, test, and deploy the code. As these agents evolve into autonomous systems that execute commands, manage dependencies, access cloud resources, and interact with other agents, their security risks extend beyond incorrect code to actions with direct consequences for software systems. Although research on these risks is expanding, it remains fragmented across areas including prompt injection, insecure code generation, supply-chain attacks, and human factors, with limited consensus on terminology, threat assumptions, and evaluation. This paper consolidates emerging research through the lens of the vibe coding workflow. We establish a reference architecture, characterise six levels of agent autonomy, and develop a threat model centred on five trust boundaries spanning developers, AI models, tools, cloud infrastructure, and the wider software ecosystem. Building on this foundation, we propose a taxonomy of twenty-one threats across nine classes. For each threat, we review the available evidence, assess proposed defences, and identify limitations. Our analysis highlights that risks increase with agents' operational authority, while most defences rely on model judgement and address isolated threats. Finally, we identify eleven research challenges, including enforceable limits on agent authority and shared benchmarks and methodologies for assessing vibe coding security.

nominations.title: Bajillion: Cryptographic Clearing for Micropayments
nominations.authors: Patrick O'Grady, Guru-Vamsi Policharla
nominations.abstract: Much of the web is funded by advertising, a model that erodes as humans delegate browsing to AI agents acting on their behalf. A natural replacement is for agents to pay for what they consume, often a fraction of a cent per request. At the scale of web traffic, this could mean tens or even hundreds of millions of payments per second. We present Bajillion, a clearing protocol for scalable micropayments. A sender signs a payment request, and an untrusted operator answers with a preconfirmation, which promises the receiver that it will be paid. Periodically, the operator closes an epoch by posting only the net effect of its payments on chain. Bajillion guarantees that a malicious operator can only omit payments -- it can never debit a sender beyond what it signed, nor misdirect a transfer. Posted balances are therefore finalized immediately and can be withdrawn. By design, senders never have to raise disputes, making it suitable for ephemeral AI agents. A receiver that is shortchanged can prove that a close omitted a preconfirmed payment, which halts the protocol and lets every user exit with its finalized balance. Requests from different senders can be processed independently, allowing the operator to parallelize up to the number of senders. We capture these guarantees in an ideal functionality for accountable clearing and prove that Bajillion realizes it.

nominations.title: A Forensic Analysis of Metadata and Information Leakage in Swedish Public Documents
nominations.authors: Noor Abo Hasan, Kajsa Linderoth, Monia L\"onn
nominations.abstract: This study investigates metadata and structural content leakage in publicly available PDF documents from 30 Swedish public-sector authorities. Using an automated collection pipeline and ExifTool-based extraction, 2,876 documents were analyzed and classified using an R0-R3 risk taxonomy. Results reveal that 48.4% of documents exhibit significant metadata exposure (R2 or R3), with significant variation across institutional tiers (p < 0.001). Longitudinal analysis across three legislative periods reveals a statistically significant reduction in metadata exposure between the baseline and post-enactment periods, yet 44.9% of documents published after the enactment of the Swedish Cybers\"akerhetslagen continue to leak sensitive metadata. Furthermore, 41.6% of documents contain incremental update layers; forensic analysis recovered verifiable text alterations, including deleted personal data and internal identifiers, from 228 of these cases. These findings highlight persistent regulatory lag and a systemic reliance on default, unsanitized document publication workflows within the Swedish public sector.

nominations.title: CNN Architecture Comparison for Malware Classification with Limited Training Data
nominations.authors: Noor Abo Hasan
nominations.abstract: Traditional malware classification methods struggle to keep pace with rapidly evolving threats. Image-based malware classification offers a promising alternative by converting malware binaries into grayscale images for analysis with deep learning. While effective, organizations often face practical constraints in acquiring sufficient training data, especially for newer threats. This thesis investigates dual-path CNN architectures with intermediate feature fusion as a potential enhancement for malware classification, with particular focus on how varying training data size affects their comparative performance against traditional single-path approaches. This research implements and compares two models: a baseline single-path using the pre-trained VGG16 architecture and a dual-path model that combines VGG16 with a custom CNN through intermediate feature fusion. Both architectures are evaluated on a binary classification task distinguishing between two malware families (C2Lop.P trojan and Dialplatform.B worm) from the Malimg dataset. Each model is trained across four different training data proportions (20%, 40%, 60%, and 80%), with three training runs per size to ensure statistical robustness, while being evaluated on complementary test sets of varying sizes. Though both architectures achieved perfect classification performance across all training percentages, the study revealed significant differences in secondary metrics including training efficiency, robustness to noise perturbation, and architectural complexity. The findings challenge common assumptions about complex architectures, demonstrating that simpler models can offer superior efficiency and robustness without sacrificing classification performance in image-based malware analysis.

nominations.title: PersonaHate: A Scalable Persona-Based Data Synthesis Pipeline for Hate Speech Analysis
nominations.authors: Xinyu Zhang, Ziqing Yang, Michael Backes, Yang Zhang
nominations.abstract: Hate speech remains a persistent and evolving threat on online platforms. The widespread use of large language models (LLMs) further intensifies this problem by making hateful content easier and cheaper to generate at scale. Although stronger hate speech detectors continue to be proposed, their performance remains uneven across target identity groups and different forms of hateful expression, partly because existing training data provides only limited coverage of these cases. Thus, we introduce PersonaHate, a scalable persona-driven data synthesis pipeline for constructing diverse hate speech datasets. PersonaHate begins with a large persona pool of 457K personas drawn from two real-world sources. Conditioned on selected personas from this pool, it prompts eight LLMs to generate hate speech across 34 identity groups and performs multi-judge annotation to obtain reliable labels. The resulting corpus contains 791K samples, from which we curate a 67K group-balanced training set. Our modular design also supports extension to new identity groups, generators, and emerging hate targets. Built upon this dataset, we evaluate two detector training strategies: training from scratch and further fine-tuning. Results show that all trained models achieve competitive performance across four widely used external benchmarks. Notably, a 184M-parameter DeBERTa-v3 model trained on PersonaHate reaches 77.5% average F1 and 79.4% average accuracy, outperforming OpenAI's Moderation API on HateBenchSet and MHS. Furthermore, fine-tuning Llama-3.1-8B raises its average F1 from 70.7% to 78.4%, a gain of 7.7 percentage points, surpassing LlamaGuard-3, Meta's official safety model based on the same Llama-3.1-8B architecture, on three of four benchmarks. These results show that PersonaHate can substantially improve the robustness and cross-dataset generalization of hate speech detectors.

nominations.title: Eight in Ten LLMs Leak System-Prompt Secrets: Nevan, an Agentic Capture-the-Flag Study
nominations.authors: Ana Clara Zoppi Serpa, Anderson Rocha, H\'elio Pedrini
nominations.abstract: We audit instruction-hierarchy enforcement across 363 text-in/text-out models from the OpenRouter catalog. The research question we answer with this experiment is which models disclose a protected secret embedded in the system prompt, and through which techniques. Each model guards a secret 16-character flag set in its system prompt, while an artificial intelligence (AI) agent (OpenCode, powered by DeepSeek V4.1 Flash), steered by a human researcher, tries to persuade it to emit the flag. The flag was exfiltrated from 296 of the 363 models, plus four models released after the initial catalog freeze, for 300 captures in total. Of these, 170 involved a non-English language pivot, most often French. Each capture shows that a model ranked a user request above its system instruction at least once. It does not show that the model provably resists untested attacks, nor that it would consistently leak semantically sensitive data, nor that it is vulnerable to harmful-content jailbreaks. For practitioners, we draw three lessons: do not store secrets in system prompts, enforce critical behavior outside the model with output validation and deterministic checks, and do not let a large language model (LLM) judge be the sole decider of consequential outcomes.

nominations.title: Hierarchical Personalized Federated Learning for Fine-Grained Intrusion Detection: A Multi-Class Analysis in Heterogeneous Attack Environments
nominations.authors: Abul Kalam Azad, Travis Atkison
nominations.abstract: Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS) play a vital role in protecting modern network infrastructures. Although Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative training without sharing raw network traffic, global models struggle with non-IID attack distributions. Moreover, practical security operations require fine-grained attack classification for targeted threat responses. To address these challenges, this paper investigates the convergence dynamics and performance of Hierarchical Personalized Federated Learning (HPFL), which combines multi-tier aggregation with client-level personalization, for 8-class, 6-class, and 4-class intrusion detection using Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) models implemented in NVIDIA FLARE on the CICIDS2017 dataset. Experimental results show that personalized HPFL models achieve micro F1-scores up to 0.9911 in the 6-class task, while the overall local accuracy reaches 0.9975 in the 8-class task. On 8-class local test sets, HPFL achieves a micro F1-score of 0.9901 and a macro F1-score of 0.8324, outperforming FedAvg (0.7176) and FedProx (0.5624) in macro F1. Cross-client evaluations demonstrate out-of-distribution generalization, with HPFL achieving a 4-class micro F1-score of 0.9294 compared with 0.9140 for standalone local models. Furthermore, distance-weighted network analysis estimates a 48.9% reduction in transmission overhead compared with conventional FL (194.4 MB vs. 380.3 MB for the 8-class task). These findings demonstrate HPFLs potential as an accurate, privacy-preserving, and communication-efficient approach to fine-grained intrusion detection in heterogeneous networks.

nominations.title: Is 4-Bit Quantization More Than Noise to a Chat Model's Safety Behaviour? Attributing Behavioural Shifts with Matched Perturbations
nominations.authors: Ege Kaya (University of British Columbia)
nominations.abstract: Chat models on phones and laptops are usually 4-bit copies of the model that was evaluated, and audits of such copies disagree about what quantization does to refusal. A 4-bit build is one of many weight perturbations of the same size, so a change in its behaviour could come from its specific rounding error or from any perturbation that large. In a pre-registered study of three 3-4B chat models, with paired tests, blind human labels and an 8-bit null, we find two 4-bit shifts of opposite sign: with a compliant reply prefilled, Qwen2.5-3B continues into harmful content more often, and on held-out jailbreaks Llama-3.2-3B complies 10.3 points less often. Matched perturbations separate the two. Shuffled and Gaussian versions of the error average close to zero, while scaling the real error, from its mirror image to twice its size, changes behaviour near-linearly. At half the real error, Llama's likelihood is almost unchanged, yet it already complies 5.8 points less often, and llama.cpp's Q4_K_M, at the same bits per weight, moves neither model. Refusal under 4-bit quantization depends on the specific rounding error, not on bits per weight or likelihood, so each build has to be compared with its original.

nominations.title: GapLeak: When Privacy-Preserving LLM-based Web Agents Become a Privacy Risk
nominations.authors: Chaklam Cheong, Tiancong Cao, Qi Li, Zelin Zhang, Jianbing Ni, Rongxing Lu, Mohammad Zulkernine
nominations.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based web agents rely on data minimization and least privilege to protect user privacy. We show that these principles are necessary but insufficient: they constrain authorized sources, but not higher-sensitivity sources that remain reachable. A website can request a field unavailable from authorized sources, creating an information gap. To complete the task, a goal-driven agent may escalate to reachable but unauthorized sources and disclose accumulated sensitive information. We formalize this vulnerability as GapLeak, where an adversary exploits a legitimate web form without prompt injection or other malicious instructions. We evaluate GapLeak on three web-agent frameworks and six LLMs from Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI across recruitment, e-commerce, travel, and healthcare. GapLeak induces an average unauthorized disclosure of approximately 37%. The information gap is the primary driver: eliminating it reduces disclosure by more than 50%. Existing instruction-level defenses based on least privilege partially mitigate the vulnerability but often reduce task success. We propose submission-time verification, which filters unauthorized content before form submission, eliminating over 96% of unauthorized disclosures while preserving task success.

nominations.title: From Token Changes to Task Failures: Bit Flips in a Shared KV-Cache Block
nominations.authors: Yuji Yamamoto, Satoshi Matsuura
nominations.abstract: In LLM serving systems with prefix caching, each KV block of a shared system prompt is held in GPU memory as a single physical copy, which every request with that prompt reads. Our earlier work measured change and showed that one bit flip in such a block changes many later responses without making them visibly degenerate. This paper extends that work by measuring how often the changed responses are wrong. Using software fault injection into vLLM serving Qwen3-8B, we flip the most significant mantissa bit or the sign bit of a value in such a block. We score responses on four tasks: code generation, short-answer questions, multiple-choice reasoning, and refusal under a policy. The fraction of changes that turned a correct response wrong depended strongly on the task: 0.023 on MBPP+ and 0.59 on held-out TriviaQA at the mantissa bit, and 0.019 and 0.60 at the sign bit. Harm fell on requests whose sampled answers are sometimes wrong, so the damage of a flip depends on how common such requests are. Harmed responses looked like ordinary errors, so a flip should be detected by checking cached blocks rather than by monitoring outputs.

nominations.title: Dressed in Authority: Practical Black-Box Jailbreaking of MLLMs via Visual Trust Bias
nominations.authors: Weihang Liu, Qianqian Xu, Yangbangyan Jiang, Zitai Wang, Zhipeng Yu, Qingming Huang
nominations.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are rapidly advancing, yet their safety remains a critical concern, especially under jailbreak attempts. Existing MLLM jailbreaks either inject fragile adversarial perturbations into irrelevant images or synthesize toxic visual cues to achieve text-driven attack intents. In contrast, a more practical MLLM jailbreak emphasizes enhancing attack efficacy directly on naturally occurring harmful image-text pairs. We address this problem by proposing Visual Trust Bias Attack (VTBA), a new jailbreak framework that exploits a previously overlooked attack surface: MLLMs exhibit an intrinsic trust bias toward authoritative visual features, which enables transferable and stealthy jailbreaks. VTBA constructs a bank of authoritative templates, matches each input pair to the most relevant one, and integrates the harmful intent into the selected layout, thereby leveraging credible visual cues to override safety refusals while preserving naturalness. We further construct a dataset of 2,500 naturally occurring image-text pairs to evaluate jailbreaks in this practical multimodal setting. Extensive experiments show that our method consistently achieves high attack success rates across strong MLLMs, revealing a severe and previously underexplored weakness in current multimodal safety alignment. Warning: This paper may contain sensitive content.

nominations.title: TetherMark: Instance-Level Watermark Authentication Against Cross-Instance Transplantation
nominations.authors: Jin Wei, Rundong Li, Li Ma, Yikai Wang, Ruihao Yang, Jianxiong Wu, Xiaoyuan Duan, Yanbo Wang, Runyu Mao, Chen Fang, Chang Xu, Ping Chen, Jun Dai, Xiaoyan Sun
nominations.abstract: Robust watermarking is commonly verified by asking whether a hidden payload remains decodable after compression, geometric distortion, or generative editing. Localized and semantic extensions may additionally check whether an expected region or category is still present. These tests establish evidence validity or content consistency, but not whether the evidence still belongs to the particular visual instance registered by its owner. We expose cross-instance transplantation: an attacker extracts or estimates valid watermark evidence from one registered image and transfers it to a different image of the same category. The message can still decode, the expected content can remain present, and the result can look natural, even though the evidence has been reassigned to the wrong instance. To enable instance-level watermark authentication, we introduce TetherMark, a post-hoc watermark that combines two complementary checks. The message check verifies an edit-robust payload, while the relation check uses secret patch-pair selection, a registered response, natural correspondence transport, and enrollment normalization to test consistency with the registered instance. The verifier accepts only when both checks pass. Across 240 test subjects, TetherMark attains 92.08% legitimate true acceptance with 9.17% and 16.25% attack success under WmForger and WMCopier, respectively, yielding the highest instance-binding balanced accuracy under both attacks.

nominations.title: From Attack Tree to Model Checker: Binding CAPEC Patterns to Verify Robotic System Security
nominations.authors: Juel Hussain (Department of Computer Science, University of Manchester, UK), Louise A. Dennis (Department of Computer Science, University of Manchester, UK), Clare Dixon (Department of Computer Science, University of Manchester, UK), Marie Farrell (Department of Computer Science, University of Manchester, UK)
nominations.abstract: Security-minded verification of autonomous and robotic systems presupposes an attacker, yet the path from a threat catalogue to a checkable attacker model is still traversed by hand. This research preview presents the theory and construction of a pipeline that mechanises it. Each leaf of an attack tree is mapped to a CAPEC attack pattern and written in first-order logic as a rule: the attacker's prerequisites imply the attack's effect. Casting the pattern as such a rule is what makes it operational - its variables can be bound to a specific system's parts, and its prerequisites can then be tested against that system under a chosen configuration of security controls. Binding is our means of verifying whether a system is vulnerable to a given attack: from a bound pattern we derive an attacker model, turn its effect into a temporal-logic property, and check that property against the system with and without a countermeasure, reporting the control that defeats the attack. We describe the signature, schemas, profiles for approach, and explore how CAPEC can support reasoning about robotics security.

nominations.title: Exploited Before It Was Fixed? Vulnerability Timelines from Open, Machine-Readable Evidence
nominations.authors: C\'edric Bonhomme, Alexandre Dulaunoy
nominations.abstract: -05-X-03), Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogs, and exploitation sightings. We introduce an evidence model implemented in Vulnerability-Lookup that selects the earliest evidence for each lifecycle event, distinguishes vulnerability-specific records, preserves date precision, and ensures traceability to original sources. Among 3,758 vulnerability identifiers with exploitation evidence, 98% have disclosure dates, while only 15.7% have patch evidence. Vendor-side dates required by VTEM are entirely absent. Most exploitation dates originate from catalog listings, including 1,041 entries associated with bulk catalog imports. After excluding these entries and ambiguous same-day observations, 59 vulnerabilities exhibit patch evidence following exploitation evidence, with a median interval of 7.6 days, predominantly between catalog listings and distributor fixes. Evidence traceability also exposes systematic measurement errors: one collector incorrectly classified exploit publications as active exploitation, accounting for 40% of initial exploitation dates, while another catalog assigned vulnerability publication timestamps to 11% of its listings. Our findings demonstrate that exploitation-to-patch intervals are computationally measurable, but their reliability depends on the availability, precision, and provenance of published evidence. We identify the additional disclosure, exploitation observation, and patch availability timestamps needed to improve vulnerability lifecycle measurements.

nominations.title: How Well Is My Artwork Protected? Predicting and Tailoring Protection against Style Mimicry by Personalization
nominations.authors: Jihye Kang, Jiwon Park, Sungwoo Hwang, Namhyuk Ahn
nominations.abstract: Protection tools add an imperceptible perturbation to each artwork so that a model personalized on it fails to imitate its style, and they apply one recipe, a protection method at a fixed strength, to every artwork. We find that the same recipe protects artworks very differently, well beyond the noise of personalization seeds, and that cheap signals predict this protection before any personalization. Because protection rises and falls together across recipes, our method, Patina, predicts the protection of every recipe from one short trial protection and gives each artwork the weakest recipe whose predicted protection reaches a chosen level. At the same level of visibility, Patina lets more artworks pass the protection threshold than any single recipe and warns the artist about artworks for which no recipe is predicted to pass it.

nominations.title: Evolution Under Fire: Evolving Agent Safety Harnesses with Adaptive Injection Stressors
nominations.authors: Yujun Wang, Yilun Liu, Jinhe Bi, Krishna Kanth Nakka, Xuebing Zhou, Hinrich Sch{\"u}tze, Yunpu Ma
nominations.abstract: Tool-using language-model agents must act on information from untrusted emails, webpages, and documents. This creates a central security challenge: malicious instructions and legitimate task directives can arrive through the same interaction channel. Existing defenses are largely hand-designed and static, making further improvements dependent on repeated manual redesign. We introduce Evolution Under Fire, a staged framework that couples safety-harness evolution with adaptive stressor evolution. Utility-constrained, Pareto-scheduled tree search evolves complete executable safety harnesses from execution evidence while keeping the task model, benchmark, tools, and evaluator fixed. Adaptive stressor evolution then discovers utility-preserving attacks that guide a subsequent stage of harness evolution. On AgentDyn with GPT-4o-mini, an evolved harness reduces attack success from 50.4% to 3.0%, improves clean and attacked utility over the initial harness, and offers a stronger security-utility trade-off than reproduced defenses. On Agent-SafetyBench with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, harness evolution reduces attack success from 82.6% to 62.0% while retaining helpfulness and runtime validity. Evolved harnesses also transfer without further evolution to Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, reducing attack success from 32.1% to 0.9% while improving attacked-task utility.
